\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements (a uniform record type, query-time aggregation,
and deterministic labels for folding) drive the design. We introduce two
abstractions that satisfy R1 and R2, operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks}), and a pluggable
intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that satisfies R3.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
\label{sec:ops}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction. An \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

Query-time stack selection directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem
from \S\ref{sec:background}. Sessions and spans are optional operation
fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree). Excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$. The predicate
$\varphi$ selects which operations participate, the stack function
$\sigma$ maps each operation to a frame sequence, and the weight
function $w$ assigns a nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
questions.

but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}

View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule

\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels, the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this through \emph{intent recognition}, mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative. The developer runs \toolname,
observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds rules, re-runs, and
iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

For structured traces such as public benchmark datasets, where action
types, tool names, and quality annotations are explicit fields, intent
recognition is unnecessary. \toolname supports
deterministic \emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from
existing ones before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records
the complete analysis configuration (data sources, mappings, predicates,
stack fields, and outputs) for deterministic replay. This dual path
explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions (which need
intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need mapping
rules). Both paths produce operations with fields, and the stack query
works identically on both.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler implemented as a Rust CLI
(Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). It reads recorded traces, not live
events. The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
fields preserved as operation fields.

Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.

\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects.
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
are complementary. AgentSight answers ``what happened during this run''
(debugging), \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across runs''
(profiling).

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets (those containing observations from
multiple semantic regions) under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets. A flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example illustrates the scale. \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
appears under 48 distinct prompt labels. The top label (\texttt{refactor})
accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.

As a robustness check, a label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within
each session) confirms the separation is not random ($p = 0.001$). This
result assumes label quality, a dependency we validate in RQ3 for
structured traces (V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 datasets). For the
regex-derived labels on real sessions, the permutation test confirms
non-random separation, but direct quality assessment against
human-annotated ground truth remains future work.

RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
objects. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
stack fields. A flat GROUP BY on a single label cannot produce these views because
different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens.

These quantitative results translate to concrete aggregate insights.
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot
produce this distribution without external aggregation. The \texttt{files} view shows
\texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across different sessions repeatedly
accessing the same source files, aggregated into a single wide bar that
a timeline shows as isolated events. The \texttt{network} view
attributes domain contacts to prompt categories, and the \texttt{files}
view identifies accesses outside the project root, supporting security
auditing.

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

RQ2 asks whether the profiler's top groups correspond to real labeled
problems, specifically whether categories that concentrate failures, safety
violations, or wasted effort surface at the top of ranked output. The
methodology is analogous to injecting known
bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation. Public benchmark datasets
provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
positives.

\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
The benchmark uses six tasks across four datasets (AgentRewardBench
looping and side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect
and redundant step, and OSWorld-Human group start), totaling 34{,}539 operations and
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (\S\ref{sec:design}). Fixed-session
drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
tasks, confirming that profilers and debuggers are complementary.

Statistical validation supports these comparisons. Bootstrap
(10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials) confirm
stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\% prevalence/group-size null on all
six tasks.

\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}

Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level. Quality
assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
remains future work.

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events), of which 82{,}886 hit
the label cache and 35{,}136 require real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. All requests complete without tag failures. On a
fixed set of 300 redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B)
all produce 900/900 syntactically valid outputs with p95 latencies of
23, 18, and 31\,ms respectively.

\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation.
For each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.

Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure
exceeds 0.7, indicating strong agreement between mapping-derived and
native labels. The two low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have
atypical action vocabularies that the held-out mapping rules do not
cover. Mapping reduces unique stacks on 6/9 datasets with zero negative
regressions.

A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
F1~1.0). These baseline comparisons support field derivation as a guarded configuration
step, not automatic intent discovery.

Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
on the same 13{,}265 operations and produce identical V-measure on 7/9
datasets, with the two divergent datasets differing by $\leq$0.17.
Mapping quality is robust to minor rule variations on well-covered
action vocabularies. Direct cross-backend comparison between the regex
and LLM taggers on the same free-form prompts remains future work.

Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set. The 3B model produces a broader
vocabulary (328 unique prompt labels) but includes noisy entries. A
display-governance pipeline reduces unique labels from 1{,}546 to
1{,}364 through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage
from 93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw labels. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy. The ground-truth and
cross-backend checks above provide that.

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations), and all produce
identical output with median runtime 1.6\,s per spec.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage. Profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain. Samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging. \toolname complements them with cross-session
aggregate profiling. Datadog LLM Observability and Laminar Signals take
steps toward semantic aggregation by clustering user messages or
extracting structured events, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions}, not \emph{resource attribution}.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas~\cite{agentatlas} argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying
which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most
budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions, operations and operation stacks, close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information that flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

Profilers and debuggers are complementary. Fixed-session drilldown finds
a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks (RQ2), while the profiler
identifies which categories deserve attention. \toolname supports both
by including or excluding session fields in the stack query. The
profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is designed
for automated consumption by analysis agents, though evaluation of
agent-driven diagnosis is future work.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data. Multi-project
evaluation and trace-ecosystem integration (importing OpenTelemetry and
LangSmith traces as operations) are the most impactful next steps.

\end{document}

## Report: Problem Framing Evaluation

2. **Root cause is identified.** Line 41 names it: "过早绑定到某一种边界上" (premature binding to a single boundary). This is structural, not just symptomatic.

3. **Multi-dimensional.** The problem statement covers failure diagnosis, safety, quality, looping, human-boundary recovery, and cross-dataset generality. Not single-dimension.

4. **Scope discipline is excellent.** Lines 67-68 and the limitations section (676-702) explicitly disclaim what the paper does *not* claim. This is unusually honest framing.

---

### Problems found

**Issue 1: The abstract opens with symptoms, not pain (IMPORTANT)**

Lines 38-41:
> "AI agent 的执行历史已经不再只是一次 prompt 或一棵 trace tree。一个真实轨迹可能同时包含用户意图、LLM 响应、tool call、API 调用..."

This is a feature list of what traces contain, not a painful consequence. A reviewer reads this and thinks "so what?" The pain (you can't fold the same trace at different depths for different questions) doesn't land until line 41, four sentences in. By that point, the abstract has already pivoted to the solution (line 43).

**Suggestion:** Open with the consequence: a developer trying to answer "which tool-call family causes the most failures" cannot do so in current tools without manually drilling through hundreds of sessions. Then state why: fixed hierarchies.

---

**Issue 2: Section 1 (问题) is too abstract — no concrete scenario (IMPORTANT)**

Lines 73-76 list questions a developer might ask ("哪类任务导致最多重复点击，哪些 GUI 轨迹反复输入..."), but these are enumerated generically. There is no concrete walkthrough showing *what actually goes wrong* when someone tries to answer one of these questions with an existing tool.

**Suggestion:** Pick one of the six RQ2 tasks (e.g., looping detection in AgentRewardBench) and show concretely: in a session-based tool, the developer would need to open 285 session groups; with operation-stack, 157.5. Make the reader feel the 2× wasted inspection before the solution appears.

---

**Issue 3: The abstract solution arrives too early (IMPORTANT)**

Line 43 introduces "本文提出一种更小的语义剖析模型" — the solution — after only 4 sentences of problem setup (lines 38-41). Then lines 43-49 describe the model, and lines 50-65 describe all four RQs with detailed numbers. The abstract is 80% solution/results, 20% problem.

By the checklist: "Makes the reader feel the problem before offering the solution." The current ratio doesn't let the problem breathe.

**Suggestion:** Expand the problem to 6-8 sentences before the solution. Compress the RQ descriptions (especially RQ3/RQ4 — the abstract doesn't need field-suitability synthesis or byte-stable replay details).

---

**Issue 4: Root cause restates the symptom at one level (MINOR)**

Line 41: "这两种做法都会把 profiling 问题过早绑定到某一种边界上" says existing tools bind too early. But *why* do they bind early? The deeper root cause — that agent traces mix heterogeneous object types (prompts, tools, GUI actions, processes) that don't share a common record model — is hinted at in line 39 but never stated as the structural root cause.

## Round 2a: Strongest "Not Novel" Attack

### 1. The single best attack: **The paper's own related work concedes the insight**

The paper states its insight as: "agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that flame-graph folding requires" (lines 32–34, 124–128).

The related work section then says this about existing profiling tools:

> "Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived events. **These systems support query-time aggregation, so AgentPProf does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone.**" (lines 706–712)

The paper explicitly surrenders the "two abstractions" half of its insight — query-time aggregation over weighted records with tag-derived frames is what pprof already does. What remains is "intent recognition restores deterministic labels." But that's not an insight about profiling architecture; it's a statement that NLP classification exists and can produce labels. The paper itself treats intent recognition as a pluggable engineering component (regex, LLM tagger, K-Means — lines 324–345), not a novel mechanism. The regex tagger is admitted to take "5–10 rounds" of manual iteration (line 325).

So the contribution collapses to: **"If you label agent prompts, you can use existing profiling techniques."** That's `GROUP BY semantic_label` with the prior art's own machinery.

### 2. Supporting evidence

- **pprof tagroot/tagleaf** already lets users inject arbitrary labels as pseudo stack frames. The operation/operation-stack abstraction is isomorphic to pprof's sample-with-labels/tag-derived-stack model. The paper acknowledges this at line 708.
- **Perfetto's SQL-based trace processor** already supports arbitrary query-time aggregation over heterogeneous trace events with derived columns. This is precisely R2.
- **Datadog and Laminar** already do intent-level clustering on agent traces (lines 87–91). The paper distinguishes "input distribution" from "resource attribution," but propagating a cluster label to downstream spans is engineering (label inheritance), not a new abstraction.
- The RQ2 evaluation compares operation-stack against flat and fixed-session baselines, but **never compares against pprof with tagroot applied to the same labeled data**. If pprof tagroot produces similar flame graphs from the same labeled operations, the "two abstractions" contribute nothing beyond what pprof already provides.

### 3. Checklist pattern match — weak

The insight tries to match **Pattern 1 (Structural mismatch):** "Fixed session/span hierarchies don't match the cross-session aggregation need." The mismatch is real. But the checklist says the insight must be **non-obvious** and **separable from the system**. The mismatch diagnosis ("sessions are boundaries, not categories") is sound, but the proposed resolution (label events, then group-by) is the obvious first thing any engineer would try. The checklist's "non-obvious" test: "A reviewer should think 'that's not what I would have assumed.'" Labeling prompts and grouping by label *is* what most engineers would assume.

The insight also fails the **generality** test for OSDI-level (checklist workshop vs. OSDI table): "changes how community thinks about a class of systems" vs. "specific gap, specific solution." The two-abstraction model doesn't generalize beyond agent traces — it's pprof's model applied to a new domain. That's workshop scope.

### 4. What would make the insight stronger

The paper needs to identify something that pprof-with-labels **cannot** do. Candidates:
- **The label-derivation problem is structurally different from CPU profiling** in a way that changes the profiling model (not just adds a preprocessing step). If intent recognition must be iterative, interactive, and quality-validated against hidden oracles, that's a feedback loop that traditional profilers don't have — but the paper treats it as a pluggable preprocessing box.
- **The evaluation methodology** (hidden-label localization as profiler scoring) is genuinely novel and has no pprof analogue. But the paper buries this under the "two abstractions" framing instead of making it the insight.
- **Show that pprof tagroot is insufficient** — e.g., because recursive multi-field stacks, predicate filtering, and view-weight selection require model changes that tagroot can't express. The paper never runs this comparison.</result>

file.content:
\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}. The same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. Prompts are natural language and
lack deterministic identifiers. Tool calls, GUI
actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes. This
  subsumes diagnostic views: failure, safety, and quality labels are
  fields that participate in the same aggregation.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

2. **R3 (intent recognition) is not just preprocessing — it's the key enabler that makes the model work**, and the paper should integrate it into the insight rather than treating it as a separate plug-in box.

elements are interdependent: labels without uniform records produce

stacks lock the hierarchy at ingestion time.

## Round 2c: Re-attack Report

### 1. Is the defense effective against the original attack?

**Partially.** The "no inherent call stack" argument (§2.3 lines 204–212) effectively neutralizes the pprof-tagroot attack. The distinction is precise and correct: pprof tagroot augments an execution stack; agent traces have no execution stack to augment. A reviewer cannot dismiss this as "just use pprof" anymore. The interdependence argument in ¶5 (lines 108–110) — "labels without uniform records produce GROUP BY but not recursive flame graphs; records without query-time stacks lock the hierarchy at ingestion time" — also works. It preempts the "just GROUP BY" reduction.

However, the defense opens a new vulnerability.

### 2. Strongest remaining attack

**The insight is now correctly stated but borderline obvious to anyone who has built a profiler.** The "no inherent call stack" observation is true but not surprising. Any systems engineer who tried to apply flame graphs to agent traces would discover within an hour that (a) there's no call stack, (b) you need to construct one from fields, and (c) prompts need deterministic labels. The paper argues these three elements are "jointly necessary" — but that's a completeness proof, not a surprise. The checklist's non-obvious test: "A reviewer should think 'that's not what I would have assumed.'" A profiler engineer *would* assume exactly this.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions
  plus intent recognition.}
  We show that agent traces lack the inherent call stack that makes CPU
  flame graphs work. Uniform operation records, query-time stack
  projections, and intent-derived deterministic labels are jointly
  necessary to close this gap; any two without the third fall back to
  either flat GROUP BY or fixed-hierarchy debugging
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation via hidden-label localization.}
  We propose scoring profiler output against hidden ground-truth
  trajectory labels, analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU
  profiler evaluation. On 325 real sessions, semantic labels separate
  90\% of system-effect weight that flat views merge (RQ1). On four
  public datasets, operation-stack profiling localizes hidden labeled
  problems with 90\% less work than flat summaries and 45\% less
  group fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown (RQ2).
  Mapping-derived labels agree with ground-truth annotations on 7/9
  held-out datasets (RQ3) (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================

## Round 5 — Reviewer Stress Test

### 1. Can you easily write a reject?

**With difficulty.** The paper has a clear problem, a clean model, and solid quantitative evidence. The easiest reject angles (novelty, evaluation methodology) have been partially preempted by careful scoping and honest limitations. But a reject is constructable — it targets the gap between the two evaluation worlds (real sessions and public datasets) and the unvalidated intent-recognition link.

### 2. Best reject argument

**Paragraph 1 — The insight is a sound engineering decomposition, not a research contribution.** The paper's core claim is that agent profiling reduces to operations, operation stacks, and intent recognition. The authors correctly note that pprof already supports query-time aggregation via tagroot/tagleaf and that Perfetto offers SQL-based trace analysis. Their distinction — "agent traces have no execution stack to augment" — is accurate but does not change the profiling model in a fundamental way. The operation/operation-stack abstraction is isomorphic to pprof's sample-with-labels/tag-derived-stack model applied to a new domain. A competent engineer who decided to build flame graphs for agent traces would arrive at this decomposition within a day. The interdependence argument (lines 107–112) is a completeness observation, not a surprise.

**Paragraph 2 — The evaluation has a critical disconnection.** RQ1 (the strongest result — 90% mixed weight separated) runs on 325 real sessions with regex-derived labels whose quality against human ground truth is explicitly unvalidated (line 496: "direct quality assessment against human-annotated ground truth remains future work"). The paper's central motivating scenario — a developer profiling their own agent sessions — is evaluated only with unvalidated labels. The public-dataset evaluation, while rigorous, tests a different pipeline (mapping rules on structured traces). No experiment tests intent recognition quality on free-form prompts against ground truth, which is the hardest and most novel part of the system.

For a workshop paper this is acceptable, but the abstract's "reduces inspection work by 90%" framing oversells by selecting the weaker baseline for the headline.

The paper does both (90% mixed weight, stack-depth sweep showing 417× fragmentation with fixed sessions). The mismatch is real even if the resolution is straightforward.

A workshop paper is allowed to defer ground-truth validation of the free-form path. The two evaluation worlds address different claims (RQ1: separation matters; RQ2: the profiler model works on labeled traces).

### 4. Remaining framing weaknesses (not fatal)

- **Abstract headline number cherry-picks the weak baseline.** "90% less inspection work" is vs. flat. The 45% group-reduction vs. fixed-session is more informative and defensible. Reviewers will notice.

- **The "profilers and debuggers are complementary" conclusion** is well-stated but the paper doesn't test this complementarity. It's asserted from the WTFP counterexample, not demonstrated as a workflow.

### 5. Overall assessment

**Workshop paper: Yes, strong enough.** The problem is real, the model is clean, the evaluation covers multiple dimensions with honest scoping and counterexamples. The structural-mismatch insight is at the right level for a workshop — specific gap, specific solution, initial but multi-faceted evidence. The careful limitation framing (Pareto tradeoff not dominance, future work on label quality, explicit counterexamples) is above-average for workshop submissions.

**Full paper: Not yet.** The evaluation disconnection (real sessions with unvalidated labels vs. public datasets with mapping rules) needs to be closed. ## 当前状态总结

### 做了什么

对 `docs/agentpprof-paper/main.tex`（英文 ACM sigconf 论文）跑完了 5 轮 idea refinement，共 **15 处编辑**，论文始终编译通过，保持 7 页。

### 论文的核心故事

**问题：** AI agent 轨迹没有像 CPU profiling 那样的跨 session 聚合能力。现有工具（LangSmith、Langfuse、Phoenix）把事件固定在 session/span 树里，能调试单次执行，但无法按语义类别（review、debug、test）做跨 session 的资源归因。

**洞察：** 与 CPU profiling 的结构性差异 — agent 轨迹根本没有内在的 call stack。需要三个相互依赖的要素：
1. **operation**（统一的加权记录，取代 call-stack sample）
2. **operation stack**（查询时的字段投影，取代 execution stack）
3. **intent recognition**（恢复 flame graph 折叠所需的确定性标签）

三者缺一不可：没有标签 → 90% 权重混在一起；没有查询时 stack → 层级在采集时锁死。

**贡献：**
1. 洞察 + 模型（两个抽象 + intent recognition 的联合必要性）
2. AgentPProf 系统（Rust CLI，可插拔标签后端）
3. Hidden-label localization 评估方法（类似 CPU profiler 注入已知瓶颈）

**结果：** 325 个真实 session 上语义标签分离 90% 混合权重；4 个公开数据集上 operation-stack profiling 比 flat summary 减少 90% inspection work，比 fixed-session drilldown 减少 45% group fragmentation。

### 5 轮改了什么

| 轮次 | 焦点 | 关键改动 |
|------|------|---------|
| R1 问题定义 | 问题太单一维度 | 加入 failure/safety/quality 维度；补充 Datadog/Laminar 的结构性原因；abstract 加痛点句 |
| R2 洞察对抗 | "这不就是 pprof + 标签吗" | 引入 "没有内在 call stack" 结构性区分；三要素联合必要性用 RQ1 数据支撑；升级评估方法为贡献 |
| R3 贡献/目标 | C2 artifact-first, C3 太复合 | C2 改为 "realizes this model"；C3 升级为方法论贡献 + 加入 actionability |
| R4 对齐检查 | RQ3 标题不匹配；actionability 孤立 | RQ3 改名为 "How Reliable Are the Derived Labels?"；C3 锚定 actionability |
| R5 压力测试 | 数字只挑弱 baseline | intro 补上 fixed-session 对比数字 |

### 最强的剩余弱点（非 framing 问题，不在本轮范围）

1. **图是占位符** — 一篇关于可视化的论文没有真实 flame graph 截图
2. **评估断层** — 真实 session 用未验证的 regex 标签，公开数据集用 mapping rules，两条路径没交叉验证
3. **单项目数据** — 325 个 session 来自同一个开发项目
4. **Intent recognition 质量** — 对 free-form prompt 的标签质量是 future work

### 结论

当前 framing 对 **workshop paper 足够强**。Reject 需要 "with difficulty" 才能构造。升级到 full paper 需要：验证 intent recognition 质量、多项目数据、真实图、user study。

所有轮次日志在 `docs/tmp/idea-refinement/` 下。

# Iterative Writing Refinement

Refine a systems paper's **writing** through 10 serial review-fix rounds. Claims and framing are assumed stable. If they are not, use `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer` or the orchestrator first.

Subagents review, the main agent (you) fixes. All rounds are serial — one subagent at a time.

## First Step

Read the paper (`main.tex` or the file the user specifies). Then read `references/common-pitfalls.md` for patterns the user has flagged before.

**Always run the full cycle. NEVER stop, pause, or ask for permission between rounds.** Launch Round 0 immediately after reading and proceed through all 10 rounds without pausing. Apply fixes directly when each subagent completes, then launch the next round.

## Iteration Logs

Every round writes a log file to `writing-refinement/` inside the newest `docs/tmp/phase-*/` directory when one exists, otherwise `docs/tmp/writing-refinement/`:

```
<docs/tmp or newest phase dir>/writing-refinement/
  round-0-macro-structure.md
  round-1-micro-structure.md
  round-2-section-conventions.md
  round-3-logic-flow.md
  round-4-consistency.md
  round-5-language-sentence.md
  round-6-language-word.md
  round-7-terminology-claim-tone.md
  round-8-language-flow.md
  round-9-citations.md
```

Each log contains: date, findings, changes made (before → after), remaining concerns. On re-entry, read existing logs to resume.

## Ten Rounds (serial)

Each round: fork a read-only subagent → receive findings → apply fixes → compile → verify → next round.

**Round 0 — Macro structure.** Subagent invokes `check-paper-structure-flow` via the Skill tool with focus on Level 1 (macro). Checks: are all required sections present and correctly ordered? Is design separated from implementation? Is there an overview/architecture diagram? Are subsections balanced? You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 1 — Micro structure.** Subagent invokes `check-paper-structure-flow` via the Skill tool with focus on Levels 2-3 (micro). Checks: does each paragraph play the right role for its section? Does the abstract follow the correct paragraph structure? Does the intro have the right paragraphs for a full paper (7) or workshop (4)? Topic sentences? One idea per paragraph? You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 2 — Section conventions.** Subagent invokes `check-paper-structure-flow` via the Skill tool with focus on section-specific conventions. Checks: abstract word count and structure, intro paragraph roles, design goals paragraph, eval setup + RQ alignment, related work grouping, conclusion structure. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 3 — Logic flow.** Subagent invokes `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer` via the Skill tool. Checks: does the writing support the claims? Logic gaps? Coherent argument across sections? Intro→body→conclusion same story? You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 4 — Consistency.** Subagent invokes `audit-paper-consistency` via the Skill tool. Checks: terminology drift, cross-refs, design goals ↔ contributions, abstract ↔ intro ↔ body ↔ conclusion alignment. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 5 — Language: sentence structure.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on sentence structure. Checks: semicolons joining independent clauses, fragment sentences, subject-verb distance (>7 words), weak openings (It is / There are), colons before unlabeled lists, dangling modifiers. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 6 — Language: word choice.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on word choice. Checks: jargon inflation (count compound terms), nominalizations, vague referents (this/it without antecedent), redundant hedging, verbose phrases (in order to, utilize, due to the fact that). You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 7 — Terminology and claim tone.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on invented terms (T7) and self-attacking sentences. Checks: (1) invented terms — compound nouns that sound technical but do not exist in the field; every non-standard term must be established usage or formally defined at first use; (2) self-attacking sentences — apologies, unprompted confessions of weakness, defensive asides ("though neither is central to...", "a full soundness proof is beyond scope"); delete or move substance to Limitations. Hard boundary: scope-bearing hedges ("on the selected subset", "in our setting", "up to") are protected and must NOT be removed. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 8 — Language: flow and polish.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on flow. Checks: topic position / stress position, old-to-new information thread, paragraph transitions, register consistency across sections. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 9 — Citation gate.** Check the `.bib` file for annotation blocks (VERIFIED, REAL, PDF, ABSTRACT, USED_FOR). If any entry is missing annotations or has `REAL: unverified`, invoke `check-paper-citations` via the Skill tool for a full verification run. If all annotations are present and verified, run Pass 3 only (missing citations in .tex). You apply fixes, compile, verify page count, deliver PDF.

## Subagent Rules

- All rounds are **serial**. One subagent at a time. No parallel launches.
- Use `subagent_type: "fork"` for all review subagents.
- **Subagents must invoke the target skill via the Skill tool.** Tell the subagent: "Use the Skill tool to invoke `<skill-name>` with args `<file path and focus area>`, then follow its instructions." This loads the full skill checklist.
- Every subagent prompt also instructs: "First read `references/common-pitfalls.md` (relative to the iter-refine-writing skill directory) and check its patterns for your focus area." The pitfalls file encodes the user's past corrections; a round that misses them will be corrected again.
- Every subagent prompt must end with: **"Do NOT edit the file — only report findings as Must-fix / Should-fix / Consider with section, problem, and concrete fix suggestion."**
- After each round, compile (`make` or `latexmk`) and check for errors before starting the next round.

## Fix Application Rules

When applying a round's findings, the main agent must follow these mechanical constraints:

- **One subsection at a time.** Apply fixes subsection by subsection, never as one whole-file rewrite. If a round demands restructuring beyond one subsection, write the target outline into the round log first, then apply it in subsection-sized edits.
- **No batch text replacement on .tex.** Never use sed/regex bulk substitution on paper source; every edit is a reviewed Edit-tool change.
- **Numbers are read-only.** Language and structure rounds must not alter any quantitative value. A number changes only in the citation/consistency rounds with its source record shown.
- **Nothing lost.** After each round: `\cite{}` count must not decrease and no technical content may disappear without an explicit finding that ordered its removal. Diff-check before compiling.
- **Verify the edit landed.** Before reporting a round complete, confirm via diff that the files/sections the round claimed to fix actually changed. "Rewrote the intro" with an untouched intro is a failed round, not a finished one.

## Quality Gates

Stop iterating when:
- No Must-fix items remain
- Should-fix items are cosmetic, not structural
- Paper compiles cleanly with correct page count

## Reference Files

- `references/common-pitfalls.md` — Patterns the user has corrected before. Read at the start of every run.

16	1. Context — what exists, why it matters (1-2 sentences)
17	2. Problem — what's broken, what's the gap (1-2 sentences)
18	3. This paper — system name, what it does, how (2-3 sentences)
19	4. Results — quantitative evidence (1-2 sentences)
20	
21	The thesis ("X is the right granularity for Y") belongs in beat 3, not beat 1.
22

24	
25	**Jargon inflation.** Coined compound terms (e.g., "deny-by-default", "capability-disjoint", "blast radius") are useful for first definition but should not be repeated more than 3-5 times in a 6-page paper. 26

28	```bash

30	```
31	If any term appears >5 times in 6 pages, most occurrences can be replaced with plain language.
32	
33	**Invented terms.** AI drafting coins compound nouns that sound professional but do not exist in the field ("trusted obligation", "reference C/libbpf workflow", "production datapath"). Every non-standard term must be either established usage in the community or formally defined by this paper at first use. If a domain reviewer would ask "what is X?", replace it with plain language.
34	
35	## Section Structure
36	
37	**Design vs. Implementation.** Design sections describe WHAT and WHY (mechanism-agnostic where possible). Implementation sections describe HOW (specific kernel mechanisms, APIs, libraries). If the design section names implementation-specific APIs, move them to implementation.
38	
39	**Intro/Body redundancy.** The intro should preview (high-level, 1-2 sentences per point). Body sections should elaborate (details, examples, evidence). If both contain the same level of detail, trim the intro.
40	
41	**No \\paragraph{} headers** in short papers (6-8 pages). They clutter the layout and read like FAQ entries. Use subsection headers or flowing prose. 56	AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
57	prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
58	As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of thousands of
59	calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need aggregate
60	views: which categories of work consume the most tokens, where
61	failures concentrate, which task families trigger safety violations or

65	However, no existing observability tool provides full cross-session
66	resource attribution by semantic category. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
67	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry
68	GenAI~\cite{otel} organize events into per-execution timelines and

70	aggregation. In a real development project, the system effect
71	\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times

158	\section{Background and Motivation}
159	\label{sec:background}
160	
161	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
162	
163	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
164	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
165	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
166	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
167	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
168	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
169	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
170	
171	These models share a structural property, namely that the session or
172	span tree is the skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and
173	spans nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution
174	time. This design is effective for debugging because a developer can
175	locate a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent
176	chain to understand the execution context.
177	
178	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
179	
180	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation, \emph{folding}
181	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
182	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
183	ways.
184	
185	First, sessions are boundaries, not categories. A single session may
186	contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
187	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
188	performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
189	without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
190	(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not
191	user intent (\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping
192	by span name tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories
193	of work consumed the budget. Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect
194	like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
195	but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to
196	attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We
197	quantify this disaggregation in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).
198	
199	\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}
200	
201	CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
202	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
203	weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
204	ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
205	represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
206	\emph{deterministic}. The same code path always produces the same
207	frames.
208	
209	Agent traces break this precondition in two ways. First, prompts are
210	natural language and lack deterministic identifiers. Second, there is no
211	inherent call stack at all: agent events (prompts, tool calls, GUI
212	actions, process effects) have no runtime-determined parent-child
213	nesting analogous to function calls. Pprof's \texttt{tagroot}/\texttt{tagleaf}
214	options add label-derived pseudo-frames to an existing execution stack,
215	but agent traces have no execution stack to augment. The profiling
216	structure must be constructed entirely from semantic fields at query
217	time.
218	
219	These observations yield three design requirements:
220	
221	\begin{description}
222	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
223	  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
224	  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
225	  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
226	  objects.
227	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
228	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
229	  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the trace.
230	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes. This
231	  subsumes diagnostic views: failure, safety, and quality labels are
232	  fields that participate in the same aggregation.
233	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
234	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
235	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
236	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
237	\end{description}
238	
239	%% ===================================================================
240	\section{Design}
241	\label{sec:design}
242	
243	The three requirements (a uniform record type, query-time aggregation,
244	and deterministic labels for folding) drive the design. We introduce two
245	abstractions that satisfy R1 and R2, operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
246	operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks}), and a pluggable
247	intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that satisfies R3.
248	
249	\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
250	\label{sec:ops}
251	
252	A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
253	process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
254	abstraction. An \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
255	additive measures.
256	
257	Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
258	\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
259	\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
260	measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
261	call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
262	are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
263	
264	\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
265	\label{sec:stacks}
266	
267	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
268	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
269	representation:
270	
271	\begin{small}
272	\begin{verbatim}
273	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
274	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
275	\end{verbatim}
276	\end{small}
277	
278	\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
279	execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
280	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
281	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
282	Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
283	
284	Query-time stack selection directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem
285	from \S\ref{sec:background}. Sessions and spans are optional operation
286	fields,
287	not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
288	produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree). Excluding
289	it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
290	provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.
291	
292	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$. The predicate
293	$\varphi$ selects which operations participate, the stack function
294	$\sigma$ maps each operation to a frame sequence, and the weight
295	function $w$ assigns a nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
296	views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
297	questions.
298	
299	\begin{table}[t]
300	\centering\small
301	\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
302	but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
303	\label{tab:views}
304	\begin{tabular}{llll}
305	\toprule
306	View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
307	\midrule
308	\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
309	\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
310	\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
311	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
312	\bottomrule
313	\end{tabular}
314	\end{table}
315	
316	\begin{figure}[t]
317	\centering
318	% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig-architecture.pdf}
319	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
320	[Architecture: Agent trace files (Codex/Claude JSONL, benchmark JSONL)
321	$\to$ Parser / Importer $\to$ Intent Recognition (regex / LLM / clustering)
322	or Mapping Rules $\to$ Operations with fields $\to$ Stack query
323	$(\varphi, \sigma, w)$ $\to$ Folded stacks $\to$ Flame graph / pprof /
324	JSON]}}
325	\caption{System architecture. Local agent histories enter through
326	\texttt{agent-session} parsing. Public datasets enter as operation JSONL.
327	Both paths produce operations. The stack query and output are identical.}
328	\Description{Data flow from agent traces through parsing and intent
329	recognition to folded-stack flame graphs.}
330	\label{fig:architecture}
331	\end{figure}
332	
333	\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
334	\label{sec:intent}
335	
336	Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
337	folding still requires deterministic frame labels, the precondition
338	that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
339	this through \emph{intent recognition}, mapping free-form prompts to
340	short, stable labels before stack construction.
341	
342	The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:
343	
344	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
345	The production default. Rules have the form
346	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
347	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
348	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
349	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative. The developer runs \toolname,
350	observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds rules, re-runs, and
351	iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
352	rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
353	version-controllable.
354	
355	\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
356	For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
357	(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
358	per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
359	Labels are cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
360	
361	\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
362	TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
363	without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.
364	
365	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
366	short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
367	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
368	
369	For structured traces such as public benchmark datasets, where action
370	types, tool names, and quality annotations are explicit fields, intent
371	recognition is unnecessary. \toolname supports
372	deterministic \emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from
373	existing ones before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records
374	the complete analysis configuration (data sources, mappings, predicates,
375	stack fields, and outputs) for deterministic replay. This dual path
376	explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions (which need
377	intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need mapping
378	rules). Both paths produce operations with fields, and the stack query
379	works identically on both.
380	
381	%% ===================================================================
382	\section{Implementation}
383	\label{sec:impl}
384	
385	\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler implemented as a Rust CLI
386	(Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). It reads recorded traces, not live
387	events. The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
388	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
389	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
390	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
391	semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
392	instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
393	mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
394	Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
395	fields preserved as operation fields.
396	
397	Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
398	\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
399	\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
400	All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.

\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

spans nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution
time. This design is effective for debugging because a developer can
locate a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent

performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not

like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to
attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We
quantify this disaggregation in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}. The same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition in two ways. First, prompts are
natural language and lack deterministic identifiers. Second, there is no
inherent call stack at all: agent events (prompts, tool calls, GUI
actions, process effects) have no runtime-determined parent-child
nesting analogous to function calls. Pprof's \texttt{tagroot}/\texttt{tagleaf}
options add label-derived pseudo-frames to an existing execution stack,
but agent traces have no execution stack to augment. The profiling
structure must be constructed entirely from semantic fields at query

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]

\label{sec:design}

The three requirements (a uniform record type, query-time aggregation,

operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks}), and a pluggable
intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that satisfies R3.

\label{sec:ops}

process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction. An \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},

call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

Query-time stack selection directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem
from \S\ref{sec:background}. Sessions and spans are optional operation
fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree). Excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$. The predicate
$\varphi$ selects which operations participate, the stack function
$\sigma$ maps each operation to a frame sequence, and the weight
function $w$ assigns a nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
questions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels, the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this through \emph{intent recognition}, mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative. The developer runs \toolname,
observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds rules, re-runs, and
iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

For structured traces such as public benchmark datasets, where action
types, tool names, and quality annotations are explicit fields, intent
recognition is unnecessary. \toolname supports
deterministic \emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from
existing ones before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records
the complete analysis configuration (data sources, mappings, predicates,
stack fields, and outputs) for deterministic replay. This dual path
explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions (which need
intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need mapping
rules). Both paths produce operations with fields, and the stack query
works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler implemented as a Rust CLI
(Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). It reads recorded traces, not live
events. The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
fields preserved as operation fields.

Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.

721	\section{Related Work}
722	
723	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
724	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
725	folded-stack lineage. Profiles are weighted samples with location
726	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
727	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
728	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
729	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
730	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
731	difference is structural. Pprof's tagroot adds label-derived frames to
732	an existing execution call stack; agent traces have no execution stack,
733	so the entire profiling structure must be constructed from semantic
734	fields. The evaluation also differs: \toolname scores profiler output
735	against hidden agent-trajectory labels, a methodology with no analogue
736	in CPU profiling.
737	
738	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
739	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
740	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
741	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
742	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
743	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
744	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
745	single-execution debugging. \toolname complements them with cross-session
746	aggregate profiling. Datadog LLM Observability and Laminar Signals take
747	steps toward semantic aggregation by clustering user messages or
748	extracting structured events, but they characterize \emph{input
749	distributions}, not \emph{resource attribution}.
750	
751	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
752	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
753	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
754	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
755	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas~\cite{agentatlas} argues that outcome leaderboards
756	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
757	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
758	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying
759	which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most
760	budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

763	\section{Conclusion}
764	
765	Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
766	that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
767	make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
768	abstractions, operations and operation stacks, close this gap once
769	intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
770	confirms that semantic profiling separates information that flat views merge,
771	localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
772	fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
773	ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.
774	
775	Profilers and debuggers are complementary. Fixed-session drilldown finds
776	a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks (RQ2), while the profiler
777	identifies which categories deserve attention. \toolname supports both
778	by including or excluding session fields in the stack query. The
