All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.

\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects.
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
are complementary. AgentSight answers ``what happened during this run''
(debugging), \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across runs''
(profiling).

%% ===================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We organize the evaluation around three research questions.

\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Public labeled trace families. All traces are real agent or
human executions. The bottom four rows provide oracle labels for RQ2.}
\label{tab:datasets}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}p{0.15\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}}
\toprule
Family & Native labels & Access & Trace origin & Eval.\ role \\
\midrule
WebLINX~\cite{weblinx}, Mind2Web~\cite{mind2web}, AgentTrek~\cite{agenttrek}, WebShop~\cite{webshop} & Web actions, tasks, rewards & HF / public & Real web agents & Coverage \\
API-Bank~\cite{apibank}, ToolBench~\cite{toolbench}, tau-bench~\cite{taubench} & API calls, outcomes & HF / JSONL & Real API agents & Coverage \\
SWE-agent~\cite{sweagent} & Issue trajectories & HF viewer & Real coding agent & Coverage \\
AndroidCtrl~\cite{androidcontrol}, GUI-Odyssey~\cite{guiodyssey}, ScaleCUA~\cite{scalecua} & Mobile/GUI actions & Public/HF & Real mobile agents & Coverage \\
\midrule
AgentRewardBench~\cite{agentrewardbench} & Success, side-effect, looping & HF annotations & Real BrowserGym agents & RQ2 tasks \\
SATraj-OS~\cite{safactory} & Safety, reward, attack type & HF config & Real desktop agents & RQ2 task \\
OSWorld-Human~\cite{osworldhuman} & Human grouped-action traces & GitHub JSON & Real human OS use & RQ2 task \\
AgentNet~\cite{agentnet} & Step correctness, redundancy & HF JSONL & Real desktop agents & RQ2 tasks \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets (those containing observations from
multiple semantic regions) under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets. A flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example illustrates the scale. \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
appears under 48 distinct prompt labels. The top label (\texttt{refactor})
accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.

As a robustness check, a label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within
each session) confirms the separation is not random ($p = 0.001$). This
result assumes label quality, a dependency we validate in RQ3 for
structured traces (V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 datasets). For the
regex-derived labels on real sessions, the permutation test confirms
non-random separation, but direct quality assessment against
human-annotated ground truth remains future work.

RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
objects, validating R1. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
stack fields. A flat GROUP BY on a single label cannot produce these views because
different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens.

These quantitative results translate to concrete aggregate insights.
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot
produce this distribution without external aggregation. The \texttt{files} view shows
\texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across different sessions repeatedly
accessing the same source files, aggregated into a single wide bar that
a timeline shows as isolated events. The \texttt{network} view
attributes domain contacts to prompt categories, and the \texttt{files}
view identifies accesses outside the project root, supporting security
auditing.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
[Flame-graph screenshots: tokens view (top) and files view (bottom)
showing budget distribution and file-access patterns across sessions]}}
\caption{Real flame graphs from a development project.
Top: \texttt{tokens} view (width = token count).
Bottom: \texttt{files} view (width = file-operation count).}
\Description{Two flame graphs showing token budget and file access
distribution across semantic prompt categories.}
\label{fig:flamegraphs}
\end{figure}

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

RQ2 asks whether the profiler's top groups correspond to real labeled
problems, specifically whether categories that concentrate failures, safety
violations, or wasted effort surface at the top of ranked output. The
methodology is analogous to injecting known
bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation. Public benchmark datasets
provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
positives.

\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
The benchmark uses six tasks across four datasets (AgentRewardBench
looping and side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect
and redundant step, and OSWorld-Human group start), totaling 34{,}539 operations and
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

\paragraph{Localization results.}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.
``---'' = group count varies by task; no single median is reported.}
\label{tab:localization}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
\midrule
flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (\S\ref{sec:design}). Fixed-session
drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
tasks, confirming that profilers and debuggers are complementary.

Statistical validation supports these comparisons. Bootstrap
(10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials) confirm
stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\% prevalence/group-size null on all
six tasks.

\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}

Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Are the Derived Labels?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level. Quality
assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
remains future work.

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events), of which 82{,}886 hit
the label cache and 35{,}136 require real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. All requests complete without tag failures. On a
fixed set of 300 redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B)
all produce 900/900 syntactically valid outputs with p95 latencies of
23, 18, and 31\,ms respectively.

\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation.
For each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Leave-dataset-out mapping quality. V-measure between
mapping-derived \texttt{phase} and native \texttt{action} labels.
13{,}265 operations from the four oracle-rich families
across 9 held-out evaluations.}
\label{tab:vmeasure}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Held-out dataset & Ops & V-measure & Boundary F1 \\
\midrule
mind2web & 774 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
webshop-expert & 2{,}504 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
swe-agent & 496 & 0.926 & 0.962 \\
weblinx-chat & 500 & 0.872 & 0.860 \\
agenttrek & 200 & 0.862 & --- \\
gui-odyssey & 7{,}868 & 0.811 & 0.842 \\
android-control & 9 & 0.716 & 0.727 \\
toolbench & 866 & 0.134 & 0.353 \\
api-bank & 48 & 0.000 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure
exceeds 0.7, indicating strong agreement between mapping-derived and
native labels. The two low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have
atypical action vocabularies that the held-out mapping rules do not
cover. Mapping reduces unique stacks on 6/9 datasets with zero negative
regressions.

A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
F1~1.0). These baseline comparisons support field derivation as a guarded configuration
step, not automatic intent discovery.

Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
on the same 13{,}265 operations and produce identical V-measure on 7/9
datasets, with the two divergent datasets differing by $\leq$0.17.
Mapping quality is robust to minor rule variations on well-covered
action vocabularies. Direct cross-backend comparison between the regex
and LLM taggers on the same free-form prompts remains future work.

Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set. The 3B model produces a broader
vocabulary (328 unique prompt labels) but includes noisy entries. A
display-governance pipeline reduces unique labels from 1{,}546 to
1{,}364 through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage
from 93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw labels. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy. The ground-truth and
cross-backend checks above provide that.

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations), and all produce
identical output with median runtime 1.6\,s per spec.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage. Profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is structural. Pprof's tagroot adds label-derived frames to
an existing execution call stack; agent traces have no execution stack,
so the entire profiling structure must be constructed from semantic
fields. The evaluation also differs: \toolname scores profiler output
against hidden agent-trajectory labels, a methodology with no analogue
in CPU profiling.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging. \toolname complements them with cross-session
aggregate profiling. Datadog LLM Observability and Laminar Signals take
steps toward semantic aggregation by clustering user messages or
extracting structured events, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions}, not \emph{resource attribution}.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas~\cite{agentatlas} argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying
which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most
budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions, operations and operation stacks, close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information that flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

Profilers and debuggers are complementary. Fixed-session drilldown finds
a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks (RQ2), while the profiler
identifies which categories deserve attention. \toolname supports both
by including or excluding session fields in the stack query. The
profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is designed
for automated consumption by analysis agents, though evaluation of
agent-driven diagnosis is future work.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data. Multi-project
evaluation and trace-ecosystem integration (importing OpenTelemetry and
LangSmith traces as operations) are the most impactful next steps.

\bibliographystyle{ACM-Reference-Format}
\bibliography{references}

\end{document}

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative. The developer runs \toolname,
observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds rules, re-runs, and
iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

### 2. Intro

Opens with a goals/requirements paragraph mapping back to motivation (lines 233–237: "The three requirements…drive the design"). Each subsection addresses one requirement by name in its title (e.g., "Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)"). ✓

**Should-fix.** The evaluation section (line 397) opens directly with data setup but does not state the metrics or baselines upfront. The reader encounters metrics (AP, R@5, Work@5, WTFP, V-measure) piecemeal across RQ1, RQ2, and RQ3. A one-sentence metrics overview after the data paragraph would help: e.g., "We measure semantic separation (mixed-weight percentage), localization quality (AP, recall, work-to-first-positive), and label agreement (V-measure, boundary F1)."

It mentions evaluation results but not the *methodological* novelty of scoring profiler output against hidden trajectory labels, which was elevated as a contribution. A half-sentence addition would close this.

Good question. Let me reflect honestly on the current state before rewriting.

## My diagnosis

The abstract and intro are **structurally correct** (4-beat, right paragraph roles) but **read like a well-organized technical report, not a top-venue paper**. Specific problems:

**Abstract:**
- Beat 3 (lines 32-40) is a **definition dump**: "An operation is..., An operation stack is..., AgentPProf implements..." This reads like a README, not a thesis. OSDI abstracts state ONE crisp claim, not three definitions.
- Beat 4 has **too many numbers** (seven). OSDI gives 1-2 headline results.
- Opening is **generic** — "AI agents produce complex traces" could start any agent paper.

**Intro:**
- ¶1 is **generic background** — no hook.
- ¶5 (insight) is **too long and leaks eval numbers** (90%, 417×). The insight should be conceptual. Evidence belongs in the eval.
- ¶6 is **too thin** after trimming — lost its purpose.
- ¶5→¶6→¶7 flow is **unbalanced**: insight has numbers, this-paper has none, contributions re-state the numbers.

I'll rewrite both, then run review cycles. Starting with the abstract.

input.old_string:
\begin{abstract}
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views, not just per-execution debugging.
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
the task categories that cause them.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.
An \emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity.
An \emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On six localization tasks
across four public datasets (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
profiling reduces group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session
drilldown (157.5 vs.\ 285 median groups) and inspection work to 9.4\% of
operations in the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries.
On 7/9 held-out datasets, mapping-derived labels achieve V-measure
above 0.7.
\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
When an AI agent runs \texttt{cargo test} 2{,}903 times across 325
development sessions, existing trace tools show a single counter---they
cannot attribute executions to the review, debugging, or refactoring
prompts that triggered them.
The obstacle is structural: unlike CPU profiles, agent traces have no
inherent call stack, so flame-graph folding has no direct analogue.
We show that three interdependent elements close this gap: a uniform
\emph{operation} record that replaces the missing sample, a query-time
\emph{operation stack} that constructs the profiling hierarchy from
semantic fields, and \emph{intent recognition} that restores the
deterministic labels folding requires.
\toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model, separates 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge on 325 real sessions.
On four public datasets with hidden ground-truth labels, operation-stack
profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and
group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
\end{abstract}

input.old_string:
%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that agent profiling differs from CPU profiling in a
structural way: there is no inherent call stack to fold. CPU profilers
aggregate because the runtime produces deterministic function frames.
Agent traces have only free-form prompts and heterogeneous events.
The key insight is that two abstractions close this gap. A uniform
\emph{operation} record replaces the missing call-stack sample, and a
query-time \emph{operation stack} (a field projection, not an execution
artifact) replaces the call stack. Intent recognition restores the
deterministic-label precondition that makes folding work. These three
elements are interdependent: without intent recognition, the same
operation stack produces stacks where 90\% of weight is mixed across
intents. Without query-time stacks, the hierarchy is locked at
ingestion time and cannot shift between task-level budget and
action-level diagnosis (fixed-session stacks inflate unique stacks by
$417\times$ in RQ1).

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a profiler built on these abstractions.
We evaluate on 325 real Codex/Claude sessions and four public
benchmark datasets with hidden ground-truth labels.

55	\label{sec:intro}

57	%% ¶1: Context + concrete pain
58	AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
59	prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
60	As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, developers need aggregate
61	views: which categories of work consume the most tokens, where failures
62	concentrate, and how cost distributes across semantic categories.
63	In a real development project, \texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times
64	across 325 sessions, yet no existing trace tool can attribute these
65	executions to the review, debugging, or refactoring prompts that
66	triggered them.
67	
68	%% ¶2: Gap
69	LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
70	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
71	events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
72	not cross-session aggregation by semantic category.
73	
74	%% ¶3: Root cause
75	CPU profilers solved the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
76	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
77	into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
78	\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
79	Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
80	language, and
81	two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters
82	(\S\ref{sec:background}).
83	
84	%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail

86	Observability clusters user messages by

88	and Laminar extracts structured signals from
89	traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} Both characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
90	questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
91	consume 40\% of the token budget''). The gap is architectural:
92	clustering operates at the request level and does not propagate labels
93	to downstream system effects, so failures and costs triggered by a
94	category remain unattributed.

100	call-stack sample. A query-time \emph{operation stack}---a field
101	projection, not an execution artifact---replaces the call stack itself.
102	And \emph{intent recognition} restores the deterministic labels that
103	folding requires. Remove any one element and the model degrades: without
104	labels, aggregation mixes intents. Without query-time stacks, the
105	hierarchy is locked at ingestion.

130	  produces output (pprof, SVG, JSON) consumable by both developers and

# Paper Structure and Flow Check

Check a systems paper's structure at macro and micro levels. Report findings without editing.

## First Step

Read the paper. Determine the paper type by page count or venue:
- 12-14 pages → read `references/full-paper-12p.md`
- 6 pages → read `references/workshop-paper-6p.md` (inherits from full paper, lists only differences)
- 2 pages → read `references/extended-abstract-2p.md`

Then check at three levels.

## Level 1: Macro Structure

Compare the paper's section list against the template for its type. Check:
- Are all required sections present? Any missing?
- Is the ordering correct?
- Is Background separate from Motivation (full paper) or merged (workshop)?
- Does Design open with goals/requirements/principles + system overview?
- Does Design include an architecture diagram?
- Is Design separated from Implementation?
- Are subsections balanced in length?
- Is page budget roughly correct per section?

## Level 2: Paragraph Roles

For each section, check whether paragraphs play the correct roles as defined in the template. Focus especially on:

- **Abstract:** Does it follow the sentence-role structure? Correct word count? Does every abstract sentence map to an intro paragraph with the same claims, numbers, and terminology (no concept debuting in the abstract, no logic jumps)?
- **Introduction:** Are all required paragraph roles present (¶1 background, ¶2 problem, ¶4 existing solutions, ¶5 insight, ¶6 this paper, ¶7 contributions — never merged)? If ¶3 (root cause) is absent, is the cause still named at the end of ¶2 when ¶5's insight answers one? If ¶5b (challenges) is present, does ¶6 answer its challenges one-for-one? Does each paragraph's first sentence state that paragraph's topic? Are transitions at the start of new paragraphs, not the end of previous ones? Does ¶1 give background (not hook/problem)? Does ¶5 state the insight separately from the system?
- **Design:** Does it open with design goals? Is each subsection one design decision with why-before-what?
- **Evaluation:** Does each subsection correspond to a research question? Is there a setup paragraph?

## Level 2.5: Subsection Naming

Subsection titles must follow these conventions:
- **Noun phrases only.** Not questions ("Why X?"), not claims ("X Stops Y"), not verbs ("Implementing X").
- **Parallel structure within a section.** If one subsection is "Threat Model", siblings should be similar noun phrases ("Per-Tool Sandboxing", "Pipeline Composition"), not mixed styles.
- **Descriptive of content, not argument.** The title says what's IN the subsection, not what point it makes.
- **No "How" / "Why" / "What" question-style titles.**
- **No redundant system name.** Don't repeat the system name in every subsection title.

Bad: "Why Per-Tool Confinement", "How It Stops Attacks"
Good: "Motivation", "Per-Tool Sandboxing", "Pipeline Composition"

## Level 3: Paragraph-Internal Flow

For every paragraph:
- **Topic sentence first.** First sentence states what the paragraph is about.
- **One idea per paragraph.** Split if two distinct points.
- **Why before what.** Motivation before mechanism in design paragraphs.
- **Old-to-new.** Each sentence starts with known information, ends with new.
- **Logical connectors.** Paragraphs linked by transitions (cause, contrast, elaboration).

## Output Format

```
MACRO: [section-level issue]
MICRO: [paragraph-role issue]
FLOW:  [within-paragraph issue]
```

Prioritize as Must-fix / Should-fix / Consider.

## Report

### ABSTRACT

**Must-fix 1. Abstract beat 1 is generic (lines 23–26).**
"AI agents produce complex execution traces…" is boilerplate. Every agent paper starts this way. A top-venue abstract earns the first sentence by naming a concrete pain or surprising fact.

Fix: Open with the concrete example that ¶2 of the intro already has. E.g., "When \texttt{cargo test} runs 2,903 times across 325 agent sessions, existing trace tools show a single counter—they cannot attribute executions to the review, debugging, or refactoring prompts that triggered them."

**Must-fix 2. Abstract beat 3 is a definition list, not a thesis (lines 32–40).**
Lines 35–40 read like a glossary entry: "An operation is…An operation stack is…AgentPProf implements this model with…backends…and produces…" This is README prose. A top-venue abstract beat 3 should be ONE thesis claim + system name. The definitions belong in the Design section.

Fix: Compress to one thesis sentence and one system sentence. E.g., "We show that three interdependent elements close this gap: a uniform *operation* record, a query-time *operation stack*, and *intent recognition* that restores deterministic labels. \toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model, produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON."

**Should-fix 3. Abstract beat 4 has too many numbers (lines 41–48).**
Seven distinct numbers (90%, 45%, 157.5, 285, 9.4%, 100%, 7/9). OSDI/SOSP abstracts give 1–2 headline numbers. The detail belongs in the eval section.

Fix: Keep only the two strongest contrasts. E.g., "On 325 real sessions, semantic labels separate 90% of system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets, operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45% versus fixed-session drilldown."

### INTRODUCTION

**Must-fix 4. ¶1 (lines 58–66) has no concrete example.**
The intro ¶1 was simplified but lost the cargo-test example that ¶2 (lines 72–76) still carries. Now ¶1 is context-only ("developers need aggregate views") with no hook. Meanwhile ¶2 starts with "However, no existing observability tool…" and gives the example.

Fix: Move the concrete example ("cargo test appears 2,903 times…") into ¶1, making ¶1 end on a vivid pain. Then ¶2 can focus purely on naming existing tools and their limitation without repeating the example.

**Must-fix 5. ¶5 insight (lines 101–115) leaks evaluation numbers.**
"90% of weight is mixed" and "$417\times$ in RQ1" are evaluation results, not conceptual insight. They break the insight ¶ role: insight should state a conceptual claim, evidence deferred to eval. A reviewer reads ¶5 and thinks "this mixes the argument with its evidence."

Fix: Remove the numbers from ¶5. State the interdependence conceptually: "Remove any one element and the model degrades: without labels, aggregation mixes intents across categories. Without query-time stacks, the hierarchy is fixed at ingestion and cannot shift between task-level and action-level analysis."

**Should-fix 6. ¶5 and ¶6 overlap in function.**
¶5 (insight) closes with the interdependence argument including numbers. ¶6 (this paper) re-introduces the system and gives headline results. But the insight ¶ already did part of ¶6's job by citing numbers. After removing numbers from ¶5 (fix 5), ¶6 becomes the sole carrier of results, restoring the correct balance.

**Should-fix 7. C1 contains an em-dash (line 134).**
`close this gap---any two without the third` violates the no-em-dash rule. Rewrite: `close this gap, and any two without the third fall back to either flat GROUP BY or fixed-hierarchy debugging`.

**Should-fix 8. C3 is compound (lines 142–150).**
C3 packs methodology definition + three RQ headline numbers + actionability result into one bullet. Per the pitfalls: "each item is one sentence." This one is five sentences with four distinct claims.

Fix: Keep C3 as methodology + ONE headline result. Move per-RQ numbers to ¶6 or delete them from the contributions list (the eval section carries the detail). E.g.: "We score profiler output against hidden ground-truth trajectory labels (failure, safety, redundancy, and human-task boundaries), analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler evaluation (\S5)."

**Consider 9. ¶2 (lines 67–76) repeats ¶1's problem.**
Both ¶1 and ¶2 say "no existing tool can…" Lines 61–64 say developers need aggregate views. Lines 67–68 say no tool provides cross-session attribution. Lines 72–76 give the example. The two paragraphs could be merged or their roles sharpened: ¶1 = context with vivid example, ¶2 = name the tools that fail.

\begin{abstract}
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views, not just per-execution debugging.
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
the task categories that cause them.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.
An \emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity.
An \emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On six localization tasks
across four public datasets (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
profiling reduces group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session
drilldown (157.5 vs.\ 285 median groups) and inspection work to 9.4\% of
operations in the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries.
On 7/9 held-out datasets, mapping-derived labels achieve V-measure
above 0.7.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.

calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need aggregate
views: which categories of work consume the most tokens, where
failures concentrate, which task families trigger safety violations or
redundant effort, and how cost distributes across semantic categories.

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, no existing observability tool provides full cross-session
resource attribution by semantic category. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry
GenAI~\cite{otel} organize events into per-execution timelines and
span trees, enabling single-run debugging but not cross-session
aggregation. In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions, yet no existing trace tool can disaggregate these
executions by the semantic intent that triggered them, nor identify
which intent categories concentrate the failures.

%% ¶3: Root cause
CPU profilers solved the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters
(\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping. Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}

traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} Both characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code

consume 40\% of the token budget''). The gap is architectural:
clustering operates at the request level and does not propagate labels
to downstream system effects, so failures and costs triggered by a
category remain unattributed.

structural way: there is no inherent call stack to fold. CPU profilers
aggregate because the runtime produces deterministic function frames.
Agent traces have only free-form prompts and heterogeneous events.

\begin{abstract}
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views, not just per-execution debugging.
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
the task categories that cause them.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions---uniform
\emph{operations} and query-time \emph{operation stacks}---once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.
\toolname implements this model as a Rust profiler with pluggable
intent-recognition backends.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and
group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, both developers and
automated analysis agents need cross-session aggregate views to
identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures
concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, no existing tool provides cross-session resource attribution
by semantic category. In a real development project,
\texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times across 325 sessions, yet no
trace tool can attribute these executions to the review, debugging, or
refactoring prompts that triggered them.

%% ¶3: Root cause
CPU profilers solved the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
language, and two prompts expressing the same intent share no
characters (\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Existing agent observability tools do not close this gap.
LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
not cross-session aggregation. Datadog LLM Observability clusters user
messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} Both
characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget'').

%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that agent profiling differs from CPU profiling in a
structural way: there is no inherent call stack to fold. CPU profilers
aggregate because the runtime produces deterministic function frames.
Agent traces have only free-form prompts and heterogeneous events.
The key insight is that three interdependent elements close this gap:
a uniform \emph{operation} record replaces the missing call-stack
sample, a query-time \emph{operation stack} (a field projection, not an
execution artifact) replaces the call stack, and \emph{intent
recognition} restores the deterministic labels that folding requires.
Remove any one and the model degrades: without labels, aggregation
mixes intents across categories. Without query-time stacks, the
hierarchy is locked at ingestion.

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model.
On 325 real Codex/Claude sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels, operation-stack profiling reduces
inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and group fragmentation
by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions
  plus intent recognition.}
  We show that agent traces lack the inherent call stack that makes CPU
  flame graphs work. Uniform operation records, query-time stack
  projections, and intent-derived deterministic labels are jointly
  necessary to close this gap---any two without the third fall back to
  either flat GROUP BY or fixed-hierarchy debugging
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  A profiler that realizes this model with pluggable intent recognition
  (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
  produces output (pprof, SVG, JSON) consumable by both developers and
  automated analysis agents (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation via hidden-label localization.}
  We score profiler output against hidden ground-truth trajectory
  labels (failure, safety, redundancy, and human-task boundaries),
  analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler evaluation.
  Semantic labels separate 90\% of mixed system-effect weight (RQ1),
  operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work by 90\% versus flat
  summaries (RQ2), and mapping-derived labels agree with ground truth
  on 7/9 held-out datasets (RQ3). Profile-spec patches identify
  actionable configuration knobs on 5/6 tasks (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow to hundreds of sessions, developers need aggregate
views to identify which task categories consume the most budget, where
failures concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
the task categories that cause them.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions---uniform
\emph{operations} and query-time \emph{operation stacks}---once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.
\toolname implements this model as a Rust profiler with pluggable
intent-recognition backends.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and
group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, both developers and
automated analysis agents need cross-session aggregate views to
identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures
concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, no existing tool provides cross-session resource attribution
by semantic category. In a real development project,
\texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times across 325 sessions, yet no
trace tool can attribute these executions to the review, debugging, or
refactoring prompts that triggered them.

%% ¶3: Root cause
CPU profilers solved the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
language, and two prompts expressing the same intent share no
characters (\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Existing agent observability tools do not close this gap.
LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
not cross-session aggregation. Datadog LLM Observability clusters user
messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} Both
characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget'').

%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that three interdependent elements close this gap:
a uniform \emph{operation} record replaces the missing call-stack
sample, a query-time \emph{operation stack} (a field projection, not an
execution artifact) replaces the call stack, and \emph{intent
recognition} restores the deterministic labels that folding requires.
Remove any one and the model degrades: without labels, aggregation
mixes intents. Without query-time stacks, the hierarchy is locked at
ingestion.

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model.
On 325 real Codex/Claude sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels, operation-stack profiling reduces
inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and group fragmentation
by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions
  plus intent recognition.}
  We show that agent traces lack the inherent call stack that makes CPU
  flame graphs work. Uniform operation records, query-time stack
  projections, and intent-derived deterministic labels are jointly
  necessary to close this gap---any two without the third fall back to
  either flat GROUP BY or fixed-hierarchy debugging
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  A profiler that realizes this model with pluggable intent recognition
  (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
  produces output (pprof, SVG, JSON) consumable by both developers and
  automated analysis agents (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation via hidden-label localization.}
  We score profiler output against hidden ground-truth trajectory
  labels (failure, safety, redundancy, and human-task boundaries),
  analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler evaluation
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

## 逐句逻辑分析

### Abstract

| # | 原文 | 逻辑角色 | 问题 |
|---|------|---------|------|
| S1 | "AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects." | Context: 世界是什么样的 | OK |
| S2 | "As deployments grow to hundreds of sessions, developers need aggregate views to identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures concentrate, and which workflows waste effort." | Context: 规模化后需要什么 | OK — 目标明确了 |
| S3 | "Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events across sessions by semantic work category." | Problem: 现有工具做不到 | OK |
| S4 | "The consequence is that failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to the task categories that cause them." | Problem: 后果 | OK |
| S5 | "We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions—uniform operations and query-time operation stacks—once intent recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that flame-graph folding requires." | Thesis | **问题：跳跃太大。** S4 说"归因不了"，S5 突然说"两个抽象 + intent recognition + flame-graph folding precondition"。读者还不知道为什么 flame graph 相关、什么是 deterministic-label precondition。缺少一句 root cause 过渡。 |
| S6 | "AgentPProf implements this model as a Rust profiler with pluggable intent-recognition backends." | System | OK |
| S7-8 | "On 325 real sessions... 90%... 9.4%... 45%..." | Results | OK |

**Abstract 核心问题：S4→S5 之间缺一句 root cause。** 读者需要知道 "为什么做不到" 才能理解 "deterministic-label precondition" 是什么意思。建议在 S4 和 S5 之间加一句：类似 "The obstacle is that agent traces lack the deterministic identifiers that make flame-graph folding work in CPU profiling."

---

### Intro

**¶1 (Background):** "Agent trace 组成 + 规模化后的目标" — OK，纯 context。

**¶2 (Problem):** "没有工具能做语义归因 + cargo test 例子" — OK，纯 problem + example。

**¶3 (Root cause):** 这里有逻辑问题。

| 句子 | 说了什么 |
|------|---------|
| "CPU profilers solved the equivalent aggregation problem for programs." | CPU profiler 解决了等价的聚合问题 |
| "Flame graphs fold millions of samples... width represents cost." | 方法：flame graph |
| "The key enabler is deterministic function names..." | 关键前提：确定性函数名 |
| "Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural language..." | Agent trace 打破了这个前提 |

**问题：¶3 的第一句说 "CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem"。但读者会问：为什么突然说 CPU profiler？和 ¶2 的 agent trace 问题有什么关系？** 缺少一个连接句，比如 "The problem is not new—" 或者把 ¶3 的角色从 "CPU profiler 类比" 改成 "root cause: 为什么 agent trace 不能聚合"。

**¶4 (Existing solutions):** 

| 句子 | 说了什么 |
|------|---------|
| "Existing agent observability tools do not close this gap." | 现有工具不解决 |
| "LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix, OTel organize events into per-execution span trees..." | 它们只做单次调试 |
| "Datadog clusters by topic... Laminar extracts signals..." | 两个更近的方案 |
| "Both characterize input distributions but not resource attribution." | 它们的弱点 |

**问题：¶4 第一句 "do not close this gap" — 哪个 gap？** ¶3 说的是 "deterministic function names" 这个 CPU profiling 前提，不是 ¶2 说的 "no cross-session attribution"。"this gap" 指向不明确。应该指向 ¶2 的 aggregation gap，但 ¶3 把话题转到了 CPU profiling。

**¶5 (Insight):** "三要素关闭 this gap" — 同样的问题，"this gap" 指哪个？

---

## 核心诊断

逻辑链有一个断裂点在 **¶2→¶3 的过渡**：

- ¶2 建立了 problem："没有工具能做跨 session 语义归因"
- ¶3 突然切换到 CPU profiler，没有解释为什么 CPU profiler 和这个问题相关
- ¶4 说 "do not close this gap" 但 "gap" 的指代模糊了
- ¶5 说 "close this gap" 也模糊了

**修法：¶3 开头需要一个桥接句，说明为什么要引入 CPU profiler。** 比如：

> "This problem has been solved for programs. CPU profilers fold millions of function-call samples..."

这样 ¶3 的角色就从 "随机引入 CPU profiler" 变成 "这个问题在另一个领域已经解决了，但那个方案不能直接用"。同时 ¶4 的 "this gap" 就清楚指向 ¶2 的 aggregation gap。

# Rewrite Abstract And Intro

Reorganize the paper's existing abstract and introduction to match the venue's paragraph conventions. Start from what is on the page: reuse existing sentences wherever possible, move before rewriting, rewrite before inventing. Never invent claims, numbers, or insight wording.

## Inputs

1. The paper's current abstract and introduction (`main.tex` or the file the user names).
2. The target template, by page budget, from `check-paper-structure-flow`'s references (installed alongside this skill): `../check-paper-structure-flow/references/full-paper-12p.md`, `workshop-paper-6p.md`, or `extended-abstract-2p.md`. Read the matching file first — it defines the required and optional paragraph roles, the abstract sentence roles, and the abstract ↔ intro correspondence rule.
3. `docs/idea-story.md` if it exists — the authoritative source for insight wording, dominant claim, and contributions.
4. `docs/evaluation.md` or result records for any number that appears. Numbers are read-only: every number must come from an existing record or the current text, never from memory.

## Process

1. **Map before touching.** Label every existing intro paragraph with the template role it currently plays (background, problem, root cause, existing solutions, insight, challenges, this-paper, contributions — or "mixed"/"none"). Do the same for each abstract sentence. Produce a diagnosis: roles missing, roles merged, roles out of order, sentences sitting in the wrong paragraph, content with no role.
   Diagnose the logic chain in the same pass: the role sequence is a causal argument (background → problem → cause → existing solutions fail → insight → challenges → system → contributions), and each link must actually be argued, not just adjacent. Mark every logic jump: a paragraph that does not follow from the previous one, a concept or term used before it is introduced, an insight that does not answer the named cause, a system paragraph that does not apply the insight or answer the challenges, contributions that do not echo the insight, or a conclusion drawn from something never stated.
2. **Present the reorganization plan.** Show the mapping table (current ¶ → target ¶), what moves, what is missing and where its content will come from (idea-story, body sections — never invention), what gets cut, and whether the optional paragraphs (root cause, challenges) are warranted under their template conditions. Get the user's confirmation before editing.
3. **Rewrite the intro paragraph by paragraph.** One edit per paragraph, in template order. Keep existing citations, numbers, and established terminology. Each paragraph's first sentence is its topic sentence; transitions start new paragraphs.
4. **Derive the abstract last.** The abstract is the finished intro in miniature: compress the intro per the template's sentence roles and the strict correspondence rule (same claims, same numbers, same terms, no concept that the intro lacks, no logic jumps).
5. **Self-check and iterate.** Compile, then check the result against the template as `check-paper-structure-flow` would (required roles present and unmerged, optional roles justified, topic sentences, abstract ↔ intro correspondence). Re-walk the logic chain end to end: read the intro as an argument and confirm every link is stated — no paragraph presupposes anything not yet established, and the abstract makes no jump the intro doesn't make. Fix and re-check until required roles and the chain both pass. Report anything that could not be fixed without new evidence as open items.

## Constraints

- Insight and claim wording comes from `docs/idea-story.md` or the user; if neither exists, flag the gap instead of inventing a thesis.
- Do not add, strengthen, or renumber claims; this skill moves and tightens, the claim layer belongs to `iter-refine-writing-idea`.
- `\cite{}` count must not decrease; content removed from the intro must either exist in a body section or be listed in the report as cut.
- Check `iter-refine-writing`'s `references/common-pitfalls.md` before writing — it encodes the user's standing corrections (abstract 4-beat order, no thesis opening, no invented terms, no self-attacking sentences).

## Output

Report: the mapping diagnosis, the applied reorganization (per paragraph), the abstract derivation, self-check results, and open items. Hand off to `iter-refine-writing` for full-paper polish when the opening is stable.

\begin{abstract}
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow to hundreds of sessions, developers need aggregate
views to identify which task categories consume the most budget, where
failures concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
the task categories that cause them.
The obstacle is that agent traces lack the deterministic identifiers
that make flame-graph folding work for CPU profiles.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions---uniform
\emph{operations} and query-time \emph{operation stacks}---once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.
\toolname implements this model as a Rust profiler with pluggable
intent-recognition backends.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and
group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, both developers and
automated analysis agents need cross-session aggregate views to
identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures
concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, no existing tool provides cross-session resource attribution
by semantic category. In a real development project,
\texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times across 325 sessions, yet no
trace tool can attribute these executions to the review, debugging, or
refactoring prompts that triggered them.

%% ¶3: Root cause
The aggregation problem itself is not new---CPU profilers solved it for
programs decades ago.
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
language, and two prompts expressing the same intent share no
characters (\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Existing agent observability tools do not close this gap.
LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
not cross-session aggregation. Datadog LLM Observability clusters user
messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} Both
characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget''), because clustering at the request
level does not propagate labels to downstream system effects.

%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that three interdependent elements restore cross-session
aggregation for agent traces:
a uniform \emph{operation} record replaces the missing call-stack
sample, a query-time \emph{operation stack} (a field projection, not an
execution artifact) replaces the call stack, and \emph{intent
recognition} restores the deterministic labels that folding requires.
Remove any one and the model degrades: without labels, aggregation
mixes intents. Without query-time stacks, the hierarchy is locked at
ingestion.

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model.
On 325 real Codex/Claude sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels, operation-stack profiling reduces
inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and group fragmentation
by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions
  plus intent recognition.}
  We show that agent traces lack the inherent call stack that makes CPU
  flame graphs work. Uniform operation records, query-time stack
  projections, and intent-derived deterministic labels are jointly
  necessary to close this gap---any two without the third fall back to
  either flat GROUP BY or fixed-hierarchy debugging
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  A profiler that realizes this model with pluggable intent recognition
  (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
  produces output (pprof, SVG, JSON) consumable by both developers and
  automated analysis agents (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation via hidden-label localization.}
  We score profiler output against hidden ground-truth trajectory
  labels (failure, safety, redundancy, and human-task boundaries),
  analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler evaluation
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================

# Iterative Writing Refinement

Refine a systems paper's **writing** through 11 serial review-fix rounds. Claims and framing are assumed stable. If they are not, use `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer` or the orchestrator first.

Subagents review, the main agent (you) fixes. All rounds are serial — one subagent at a time.

## First Step

Read the paper (`main.tex` or the file the user specifies). Then read `references/common-pitfalls.md` for patterns the user has flagged before.

**Always run the full cycle. NEVER stop, pause, or ask for permission between rounds.** Launch Round 0 immediately after reading and proceed through all 11 rounds without pausing. Apply fixes directly when each subagent completes, then launch the next round.

## Iteration Logs

Every round writes a log file to `writing-refinement/` inside the newest `docs/tmp/phase-*/` directory when one exists, otherwise `docs/tmp/writing-refinement/`:

```
<docs/tmp or newest phase dir>/writing-refinement/
  round-0-macro-structure.md
  round-1-micro-structure.md
  round-2-section-conventions.md
  round-3-logic-flow.md
  round-4-abstract-intro-rebuild.md
  round-5-consistency.md
  round-6-language-sentence.md
  round-7-language-word.md
  round-8-terminology-claim-tone.md
  round-9-language-flow.md
  round-10-citations.md
```

Each log contains: date, findings, changes made (before → after), remaining concerns. On re-entry, read existing logs to resume.

## Eleven Rounds (serial)

Each round: fork a read-only subagent → receive findings → apply fixes → compile → verify → next round.

**Round 0 — Macro structure.** Subagent invokes `check-paper-structure-flow` via the Skill tool with focus on Level 1 (macro). Checks: are all required sections present and correctly ordered? Is design separated from implementation? Is there an overview/architecture diagram? Are subsections balanced? You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 1 — Micro structure.** Subagent invokes `check-paper-structure-flow` via the Skill tool with focus on Levels 2-3 (micro). Checks: does each paragraph play the right role for its section? Does the abstract follow the correct paragraph structure? Does the intro cover the required paragraph roles for its format (per the check-paper-structure-flow references — required roles always present, optional root-cause/challenges paragraphs per their conditions)? Topic sentences? One idea per paragraph? You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 2 — Section conventions.** Subagent invokes `check-paper-structure-flow` via the Skill tool with focus on section-specific conventions. Checks: abstract word count and structure, intro paragraph roles, design goals paragraph, eval setup + RQ alignment, related work grouping, conclusion structure. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 3 — Logic flow.** Subagent invokes `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer` via the Skill tool. Checks: does the writing support the claims? Logic gaps? Coherent argument across sections? Intro→body→conclusion same story? You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 4 — Abstract/intro rebuild.** No fork for this round: you (the main agent) invoke `rewrite-abstract-intro` via the Skill tool directly. If Rounds 0-3 flagged structural or logic problems in the abstract or introduction, run its full procedure (role mapping, logic-chain diagnosis, paragraph-by-paragraph rebuild, abstract derived last); write the reorganization plan into the round log instead of asking the user. If the opening passed Rounds 0-3 clean, run only the mapping + logic-chain diagnosis, log "no rebuild needed", and move on. Compile, verify.

**Round 5 — Consistency.** Subagent invokes `audit-paper-consistency` via the Skill tool. Checks: terminology drift, cross-refs, design goals ↔ contributions, abstract ↔ intro ↔ body ↔ conclusion alignment. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 6 — Language: sentence structure.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on sentence structure. Checks: semicolons joining independent clauses, fragment sentences, subject-verb distance (>7 words), weak openings (It is / There are), colons before unlabeled lists, dangling modifiers. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 7 — Language: word choice.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on word choice. Checks: jargon inflation (count compound terms), nominalizations, vague referents (this/it without antecedent), redundant hedging, verbose phrases (in order to, utilize, due to the fact that). You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 8 — Terminology and claim tone.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on invented terms (T7) and self-attacking sentences. Checks: (1) invented terms — compound nouns that sound technical but do not exist in the field; every non-standard term must be established usage or formally defined at first use; (2) self-attacking sentences — apologies, unprompted confessions of weakness, defensive asides ("though neither is central to...", "a full soundness proof is beyond scope"); delete or move substance to Limitations. Hard boundary: scope-bearing hedges ("on the selected subset", "in our setting", "up to") are protected and must NOT be removed. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 9 — Language: flow and polish.** Subagent invokes `paper-writing-style` via the Skill tool with focus on flow. Checks: topic position / stress position, old-to-new information thread, paragraph transitions, register consistency across sections. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 10 — Citation gate.** Check the `.bib` file for annotation blocks (VERIFIED, REAL, PDF, ABSTRACT, USED_FOR). If any entry is missing annotations or has `REAL: unverified`, invoke `check-paper-citations` via the Skill tool for a full verification run. If all annotations are present and verified, run Pass 3 only (missing citations in .tex). You apply fixes, compile, verify page count, deliver PDF.

## Subagent Rules

- All rounds are **serial**. One subagent at a time. No parallel launches.
- Use `subagent_type: "fork"` for all review subagents.
- **Subagents must invoke the target skill via the Skill tool.** Tell the subagent: "Use the Skill tool to invoke `<skill-name>` with args `<file path and focus area>`, then follow its instructions." This loads the full skill checklist.
- Every subagent prompt also instructs: "First read `references/common-pitfalls.md` (relative to the iter-refine-writing skill directory) and check its patterns for your focus area." The pitfalls file encodes the user's past corrections; a round that misses them will be corrected again.
- Every subagent prompt must end with: **"Do NOT edit the file — only report findings as Must-fix / Should-fix / Consider with section, problem, and concrete fix suggestion."**
- After each round, compile (`make` or `latexmk`) and check for errors before starting the next round.

## Fix Application Rules

When applying a round's findings, the main agent must follow these mechanical constraints:

- **One subsection at a time.** Apply fixes subsection by subsection, never as one whole-file rewrite. If a round demands restructuring beyond one subsection, write the target outline into the round log first, then apply it in subsection-sized edits.
- **No batch text replacement on .tex.** Never use sed/regex bulk substitution on paper source; every edit is a reviewed Edit-tool change.
- **Numbers are read-only.** Language and structure rounds must not alter any quantitative value. A number changes only in the citation/consistency rounds with its source record shown.
- **Nothing lost.** After each round: `\cite{}` count must not decrease and no technical content may disappear without an explicit finding that ordered its removal. Diff-check before compiling.
- **Verify the edit landed.** Before reporting a round complete, confirm via diff that the files/sections the round claimed to fix actually changed. "Rewrote the intro" with an untouched intro is a failed round, not a finished one.

## Quality Gates

Stop iterating when:
- No Must-fix items remain
- Should-fix items are cosmetic, not structural
- Paper compiles cleanly with correct page count

## Reference Files

- `references/common-pitfalls.md` — Patterns the user has corrected before. Read at the start of every run.
