18	\begin{document}
19	
20	\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}
21	
22	\begin{abstract}
23	AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
24	tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow to hundreds of sessions, developers need aggregate
25	views to identify which task categories consume the most budget, where
26	failures concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.
27	Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
28	hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
29	across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
30	failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
31	the task categories that cause them.
32	The root cause is structural: agent prompts are natural language, so
33	two prompts with the same intent share no identifiers that a profiler
34	could merge.
35	We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions---uniform
36	\emph{operations} and query-time \emph{operation stacks}---once intent
37	recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
38	flame-graph folding requires.
39	\toolname implements this model as a Rust profiler with pluggable
40	intent-recognition backends.
41	On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
42	system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
43	with hidden ground-truth labels (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
44	profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and
45	group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
46	\end{abstract}
47	
48	\maketitle
49	
50	%% ===================================================================
51	\section{Introduction}
52	\label{sec:intro}
53	
54	%% ¶1: Background + Context
55	AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
56	prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
57	As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, developers need
58	cross-session aggregate views to
59	identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures
60	concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.
61	
62	%% ¶2: Problem + example
63	However, no existing tool provides cross-session resource attribution
64	by semantic category. In a real development project,
65	\texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times across 325 sessions, yet no
66	trace tool can attribute these executions to the review, debugging, or
67	refactoring prompts that triggered them.
68	
69	%% ¶3: Root cause
70	The aggregation problem itself is not new---CPU profilers solved it for
71	programs decades ago.
72	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
73	into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
74	\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
75	Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
76	language, and two prompts expressing the same intent share no
77	characters (\S\ref{sec:background}).
78	
79	%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
80	Existing agent observability tools do not close this gap.
81	LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
82	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
83	events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
84	not cross-session aggregation. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} clusters user messages
85	by topic, and Laminar~\cite{laminar-signals} extracts structured signals
86	from traces. Both
87	characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
88	questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
89	consume 40\% of the token budget''), because clustering at the request
90	level does not propagate labels to downstream system effects.
91	
92	%% ¶5: Key insight
93	We observe that three interdependent elements restore cross-session
94	aggregation for agent traces:
95	a uniform \emph{operation} record replaces the missing call-stack
96	sample, a query-time \emph{operation stack} (a field projection, not an
97	execution artifact) replaces the call stack, and \emph{intent
98	recognition} restores the deterministic labels that folding requires.
99	Remove any one and the model degrades: without labels, aggregation
100	mixes intents. Without query-time stacks, the hierarchy is locked at
101	ingestion.
102	
103	%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
104	This paper presents \toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model.
105	On 325 real Codex/Claude sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
106	system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
107	with hidden ground-truth labels, operation-stack profiling reduces
108	inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and group fragmentation
109	by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
110	
111	%% ¶7: Contributions
112	This paper makes three contributions:
113	
114	\begin{enumerate}
115	\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions
116	  plus intent recognition.}
117	  We show that agent traces lack the inherent call stack that makes CPU
118	  flame graphs work. Uniform operation records, query-time stack
119	  projections, and intent-derived deterministic labels are jointly
120	  necessary to close this gap---any two without the third fall back to
121	  either flat GROUP BY or fixed-hierarchy debugging
122	  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
123	\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
124	  A profiler that realizes this model with pluggable intent recognition
125	  (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
126	  produces output (pprof, SVG, JSON) consumable by both developers and
127	  automated analysis agents (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
128	\item \textbf{Evaluation via hidden-label localization.}
129	  We score profiler output against hidden ground-truth trajectory
130	  labels (failure, safety, redundancy, and human-task boundaries),
131	  analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler evaluation
132	  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
133	\end{enumerate}
134	
135	%% ===================================================================
136	\section{Background and Motivation}
137	\label{sec:background}
138	
139	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
140	
141	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
142	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
143	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
144	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
145	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
146	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
147	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
148	
149	These models share a structural property: the session or
150	span tree is the skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and
151	spans nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution
152	time. This design is effective for debugging because a developer can
153	locate a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent
154	chain to understand the execution context.
155	
156	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
157	
158	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation, \emph{folding}
159	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
160	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
161	ways.
162	
163	First, sessions are boundaries, not categories. A single session may
164	contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
165	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
166	performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
167	without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
168	(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not
169	user intent (\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping
170	by span name tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories
171	of work consumed the budget. Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect
172	like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
173	but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to
174	attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We
175	quantify this disaggregation in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).
176	
177	\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}
178	
179	CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
180	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
181	weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
182	ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
183	represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
184	\emph{deterministic}. The same code path always produces the same
185	frames.
186	
187	Agent traces break this precondition in two ways. First, prompts are
188	natural language and lack deterministic identifiers. Second, there is no
189	inherent call stack at all: agent events (prompts, tool calls, GUI
190	actions, process effects) have no runtime-determined parent-child
191	nesting analogous to function calls. Pprof's \texttt{tagroot}/\texttt{tagleaf}
192	options add label-derived pseudo-frames to an existing execution stack,
193	but agent traces have no execution stack to augment. The profiling
194	structure must be constructed entirely from semantic fields at query
195	time.
196	
197	These observations yield three design requirements:
198	
199	\begin{description}
200	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
201	  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
202	  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
203	  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
204	  objects.
205	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
206	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
207	  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the trace.
208	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes. This
209	  subsumes diagnostic views: failure, safety, and quality labels are
210	  fields that participate in the same aggregation.
211	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
212	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
213	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
214	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
215	\end{description}

218	\section{Design}
219	\label{sec:design}
220	
221	The three requirements (a uniform record type, query-time aggregation,
222	and deterministic labels for folding) drive the design. We introduce two
223	abstractions that satisfy R1 and R2, operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
224	operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks}), and a pluggable
225	intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that satisfies R3.
226	
227	\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
228	\label{sec:ops}
229	
230	A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
231	process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
232	abstraction. An \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
233	additive measures.
234	
235	Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
236	\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
237	\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
238	measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
239	call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
240	are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
241	
242	\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
243	\label{sec:stacks}
244	
245	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
246	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
247	representation:
248	
249	\begin{small}
250	\begin{verbatim}
251	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
252	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
253	\end{verbatim}
254	\end{small}
255	
256	\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
257	execution, the stack is determined by the query. The same
258	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
259	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
260	Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
261	
262	Query-time stack selection directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem
263	from \S\ref{sec:background}. Sessions and spans are optional operation
264	fields,
265	not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
266	produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree). Excluding
267	it produces a cross-session aggregate that existing trace tools do not
268	natively support. The same data supports both debugging and profiling
269	views.
270	
271	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$. The predicate
272	$\varphi$ selects which operations participate, the stack function
273	$\sigma$ maps each operation to a frame sequence, and the weight
274	function $w$ assigns a nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
275	views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
276	questions.

312	\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
313	\label{sec:intent}
314	
315	Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
316	folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
317	that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
318	this by mapping free-form prompts to
319	short, stable labels before stack construction.
320	
321	The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends.
322	First, \emph{regex rules} are the production default. Rules have the
323	form \texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
324	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
325	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
326	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: the developer
327	runs \toolname, observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds
328	rules, re-runs, and iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This
329	typically takes 5--10 rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic,
330	reproducible, and version-controllable.
331	Second, a \emph{local LLM tagger} handles exploration or complex
332	multilingual prompts. A local model (e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via
333	llama.cpp) generates a single-word label per prompt.
334	Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity. Labels are
335	cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
336	Third, \emph{unsupervised clustering} via TF-IDF vectorization and
337	K-Means discovers natural prompt groups without predefined rules,
338	feeding rule authoring.
339	
340	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
341	short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
342	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
343	
344	For structured traces such as public benchmark datasets, where action
345	types, tool names, and quality annotations are explicit fields, intent
346	recognition is unnecessary. \toolname supports
347	deterministic \emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from
348	existing ones before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records
349	the complete analysis configuration (data sources, mappings, predicates,
350	stack fields, and outputs) for deterministic replay. This dual path
351	explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions (which need
352	labeling) and public benchmark traces (which need mapping
353	rules). Both paths produce operations with fields, and the stack query
354	works identically on both.

357	\section{Implementation}
358	\label{sec:impl}
359	
360	\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler implemented as a Rust CLI
361	(Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). It reads recorded traces, not live
362	events. The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
363	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
364	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
365	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
366	semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
367	instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
368	mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
369	Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
370	fields preserved as operation fields.
371	
372	Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
373	\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
374	\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
375	All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.
376	
377	\toolname is the offline profiling component of the broader AgentSight
378	observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
379	capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects.
380	\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
381	are complementary. AgentSight answers ``what happened during this run''
382	(debugging), \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across runs''
383	(profiling).

426	\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}
427	
428	The strongest argument against semantic profiling (cross-session
429	aggregation by intent-derived labels) is that traditional
430	tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
431	directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
432	\emph{mixed-intent} buckets (those containing observations from
433	multiple semantic regions) under different projection choices.
434	
435	\begin{table}[t]
436	\centering\small
437	\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
438	from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}

441	\toprule
442	Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
443	\midrule
444	No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
445	Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\

447	Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\

449	\end{tabular}
450	\end{table}
451	
452	Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
453	sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
454	into mixed buckets. A flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
455	executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
456	\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
457	prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
458	residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
459	sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.
460	
461	A concrete example illustrates the scale. \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
462	appears under 48 distinct prompt labels. The top label (\texttt{refactor})
463	accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
464	\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
465	others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.
466	
467	As a robustness check, a label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within
468	each session) confirms the separation is not random ($p = 0.001$). This
469	result assumes label quality, a dependency we validate in RQ3 for
470	structured traces (V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 datasets). For the
471	regex-derived labels on real sessions, the permutation test confirms
472	non-random separation, but direct quality assessment against
473	human-annotated ground truth remains future work.
474	
475	RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
476	beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
477	public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
478	objects, validating R1. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
479	fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
480	455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
481	stack fields. A flat GROUP BY on a single label cannot produce these views because
482	different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
483	budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
484	the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

487	\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share

489	\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by

493	The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that

519	\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}
520	
521	RQ2 asks whether the profiler's top groups correspond to real labeled
522	problems, specifically whether categories that concentrate failures, safety
523	violations, or wasted effort surface at the top of ranked output. The
524	methodology is analogous to injecting known
525	bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation. Public benchmark datasets
526	provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
527	human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
528	resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
529	positives.
530	
531	The benchmark uses six tasks across four datasets (AgentRewardBench
532	looping and side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect
533	and redundant step, and OSWorld-Human group start), totaling 34{,}539 operations and
534	3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
535	raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
536	visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).
537

545	\toprule

547	\midrule

558	
559	Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
560	recover all positives but require inspecting everything
561	(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
562	(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
563	2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
564	9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
565	recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.
566	
567	The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
568	serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (\S\ref{sec:design}). Fixed-session
569	drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
570	fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
571	subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
572	to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
573	dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
574	recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
575	45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
576	Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
577	tasks, confirming that profilers and debuggers are complementary.
578	
579	Statistical validation supports these comparisons. Bootstrap
580	(10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials) confirm
581	stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\% prevalence/group-size null on all
582	six tasks.
583	
584	Beyond localization, we test whether profiler output suggests concrete
585	configuration improvements. Executable profile-spec patches modify
586	stack fields, mapping rules, or rankers, then re-run over the same
587	visible operations. Five of six
588	patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
589	delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
590	emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
591	changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from stack-based
592	localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
593	(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
594	OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
595	insufficient for boundary objectives. Folding held-out boundary-derived
596	fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
597	74, with an explicit work tradeoff.
598	
599	Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
600	(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
601	misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
602	use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

606	
607	RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
608	label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
609	datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth

685	cross-backend checks above provide that.
686	
687	All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
688	re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations), and all produce
689	identical output with median runtime 1.6\,s per spec.

692	\section{Related Work}
693	
694	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
695	folded-stack lineage. Profiles are weighted samples with location
696	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
697	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
698	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
699	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
700	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
701	difference is structural. Pprof's tagroot adds label-derived frames to
702	an existing execution call stack. Agent traces have no execution stack,
703	so the entire profiling structure must be constructed from semantic
704	fields. The evaluation also differs: \toolname scores profiler output
705	against hidden agent-trajectory labels, a methodology with no analogue
706	in CPU profiling.
707	
708	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
709	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
710	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
711	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
712	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
713	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
714	single-execution debugging. \toolname complements them with cross-session
715	aggregate profiling. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} and Laminar Signals~\cite{laminar-signals} take
716	steps toward semantic aggregation by clustering user messages or
717	extracting structured events, but they characterize \emph{input
718	distributions}, not \emph{resource attribution}.
719	
720	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
721	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
722	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
723	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas~\cite{agentatlas} argues that outcome leaderboards
724	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
725	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
726	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying
727	which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most
728	budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions.
729	
730	%% ===================================================================
731	\section{Conclusion}
732	
733	Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
734	that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
735	make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
736	abstractions, operations and operation stacks, close this gap once
737	intent recognition restores deterministic labels. Scoring profiler output against hidden trajectory labels confirms
738	that semantic profiling separates information that flat views merge,
739	localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
740	fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
741	ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.
742	
743	Profilers and debuggers are complementary. Fixed-session drilldown finds
744	a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks (RQ2), while the profiler
745	identifies which categories deserve attention. \toolname supports both
746	by including or excluding session fields in the stack query. The
747	profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is designed
748	for automated consumption by analysis agents, though evaluation of
749	agent-driven diagnosis is future work.
750	
751	The main limitation is single-project real-session data. Multi-project
752	evaluation and trace-ecosystem integration (importing OpenTelemetry and
753	LangSmith traces as operations) are the most impactful next steps.

\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow to hundreds of sessions, developers need aggregate
views to identify which task categories consume the most budget, where
failures concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
the task categories that cause them.
The root cause is structural: agent prompts are natural language, so
two prompts with the same intent share no identifiers that a profiler
could merge.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions---uniform
\emph{operations} and query-time \emph{operation stacks}---once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.
\toolname implements this model as a Rust profiler with pluggable
intent-recognition backends.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and
group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, developers need
cross-session aggregate views to
identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures
concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, no existing tool provides cross-session resource attribution
by semantic category. In a real development project,
\texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times across 325 sessions, yet no
trace tool can attribute these executions to the review, debugging, or
refactoring prompts that triggered them.

%% ¶3: Root cause
The aggregation problem itself is not new---CPU profilers solved it for
programs decades ago.
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
language, and two prompts expressing the same intent share no
characters (\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Existing agent observability tools do not close this gap.
LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
not cross-session aggregation. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} clusters user messages
by topic, and Laminar~\cite{laminar-signals} extracts structured signals
from traces. Both
characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget''), because clustering at the request
level does not propagate labels to downstream system effects.

%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that three interdependent elements restore cross-session
aggregation for agent traces:
a uniform \emph{operation} record replaces the missing call-stack
sample, a query-time \emph{operation stack} (a field projection, not an
execution artifact) replaces the call stack, and \emph{intent
recognition} restores the deterministic labels that folding requires.
Remove any one and the model degrades: without labels, aggregation
mixes intents. Without query-time stacks, the hierarchy is locked at
ingestion.

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model.
On 325 real Codex/Claude sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels, operation-stack profiling reduces
inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and group fragmentation
by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions
  plus intent recognition.}
  We show that agent traces lack the inherent call stack that makes CPU
  flame graphs work. Uniform operation records, query-time stack
  projections, and intent-derived deterministic labels are jointly
  necessary to close this gap---any two without the third fall back to
  either flat GROUP BY or fixed-hierarchy debugging
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  A profiler that realizes this model with pluggable intent recognition
  (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
  produces output (pprof, SVG, JSON) consumable by both developers and
  automated analysis agents (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation via hidden-label localization.}
  We score profiler output against hidden ground-truth trajectory
  labels (failure, safety, redundancy, and human-task boundaries),
  analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler evaluation
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or
span tree is the skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and
spans nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution
time. This design is effective for debugging because a developer can
locate a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent
chain to understand the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation, \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

First, sessions are boundaries, not categories. A single session may
contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not
user intent (\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping
by span name tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories
of work consumed the budget. Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect
like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to
attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We
quantify this disaggregation in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}. The same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition in two ways. First, prompts are
natural language and lack deterministic identifiers. Second, there is no
inherent call stack at all: agent events (prompts, tool calls, GUI
actions, process effects) have no runtime-determined parent-child
nesting analogous to function calls. Pprof's \texttt{tagroot}/\texttt{tagleaf}
options add label-derived pseudo-frames to an existing execution stack,
but agent traces have no execution stack to augment. The profiling
structure must be constructed entirely from semantic fields at query
time.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes. This
  subsumes diagnostic views: failure, safety, and quality labels are
  fields that participate in the same aggregation.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements (a uniform record type, query-time aggregation,
and deterministic labels for folding) drive the design. We introduce two
abstractions that satisfy R1 and R2, operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks}), and a pluggable
intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that satisfies R3.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
\label{sec:ops}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction. An \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

Query-time stack selection directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem
from \S\ref{sec:background}. Sessions and spans are optional operation
fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree). Excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate that existing trace tools do not
natively support. The same data supports both debugging and profiling
views.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$. The predicate
$\varphi$ selects which operations participate, the stack function
$\sigma$ maps each operation to a frame sequence, and the weight
function $w$ assigns a nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
questions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig-architecture.pdf}
\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
[Architecture: Agent trace files (Codex/Claude JSONL, benchmark JSONL)
$\to$ Parser / Importer $\to$ Intent Recognition (regex / LLM / clustering)
or Mapping Rules $\to$ Operations with fields $\to$ Stack query
$(\varphi, \sigma, w)$ $\to$ Folded stacks $\to$ Flame graph / pprof /
JSON]}}
\caption{System architecture. Local agent histories enter through
\texttt{agent-session} parsing. Public datasets enter as operation JSONL.
Both paths produce operations. The stack query and output are identical.}
\Description{Data flow from agent traces through parsing and intent
recognition to folded-stack flame graphs.}
\label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this by mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends.
First, \emph{regex rules} are the production default. Rules have the
form \texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: the developer
runs \toolname, observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds
rules, re-runs, and iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This
typically takes 5--10 rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic,
reproducible, and version-controllable.
Second, a \emph{local LLM tagger} handles exploration or complex
multilingual prompts. A local model (e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via
llama.cpp) generates a single-word label per prompt.
Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity. Labels are
cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
Third, \emph{unsupervised clustering} via TF-IDF vectorization and
K-Means discovers natural prompt groups without predefined rules,
feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

For structured traces such as public benchmark datasets, where action
types, tool names, and quality annotations are explicit fields, intent
recognition is unnecessary. \toolname supports
deterministic \emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from
existing ones before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records
the complete analysis configuration (data sources, mappings, predicates,
stack fields, and outputs) for deterministic replay. This dual path
explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions (which need
labeling) and public benchmark traces (which need mapping
rules). Both paths produce operations with fields, and the stack query
works identically on both.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler implemented as a Rust CLI
(Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). It reads recorded traces, not live
events. The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
fields preserved as operation fields.

Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.

\toolname is the offline profiling component of the broader AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects.
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
are complementary. AgentSight answers ``what happened during this run''
(debugging), \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across runs''
(profiling).

%% ===================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2.
We measure semantic separation (mixed-weight percentage), localization
quality (AP, recall, work-to-first-positive), and label agreement
(V-measure, boundary F1).

\centering\small
\caption{Public labeled trace families. All traces are real agent or
human executions. The bottom four rows provide oracle labels for RQ2.}
\label{tab:datasets}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}p{0.15\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}}
\toprule
Family & Native labels & Access & Trace origin & Eval.\ role \\
\midrule
WebLINX~\cite{weblinx}, Mind2Web~\cite{mind2web}, AgentTrek~\cite{agenttrek}, WebShop~\cite{webshop} & Web actions, tasks, rewards & HF / public & Real web agents & Coverage \\

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling (cross-session
aggregation by intent-derived labels) is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets (those containing observations from
multiple semantic regions) under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets. A flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example illustrates the scale. \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
appears under 48 distinct prompt labels. The top label (\texttt{refactor})
accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.

As a robustness check, a label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within
each session) confirms the separation is not random ($p = 0.001$). This
result assumes label quality, a dependency we validate in RQ3 for
structured traces (V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 datasets). For the
regex-derived labels on real sessions, the permutation test confirms
non-random separation, but direct quality assessment against
human-annotated ground truth remains future work.

RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
objects, validating R1. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
stack fields. A flat GROUP BY on a single label cannot produce these views because
different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens.

These quantitative results translate to concrete aggregate insights.
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot
produce this distribution without external aggregation. The \texttt{files} view shows
\texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across different sessions repeatedly
accessing the same source files, aggregated into a single wide bar that
a timeline shows as isolated events. The \texttt{network} view
attributes domain contacts to prompt categories, and the \texttt{files}
view identifies accesses outside the project root, supporting security
auditing.

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

RQ2 asks whether the profiler's top groups correspond to real labeled
problems, specifically whether categories that concentrate failures, safety
violations, or wasted effort surface at the top of ranked output. The
methodology is analogous to injecting known
bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation. Public benchmark datasets
provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
positives.

The benchmark uses six tasks across four datasets (AgentRewardBench
looping and side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect
and redundant step, and OSWorld-Human group start), totaling 34{,}539 operations and
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.
``---'' = group count varies by task; no single median is reported.}
\label{tab:localization}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
\midrule
flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (\S\ref{sec:design}). Fixed-session
drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
tasks, confirming that profilers and debuggers are complementary.

Statistical validation supports these comparisons. Bootstrap
(10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials) confirm
stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\% prevalence/group-size null on all
six tasks.

Beyond localization, we test whether profiler output suggests concrete
configuration improvements. Executable profile-spec patches modify
stack fields, mapping rules, or rankers, then re-run over the same
visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from stack-based
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives. Folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Are the Derived Labels?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level. Quality
assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
remains future work.

On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events), of which 82{,}886 hit
the label cache and 35{,}136 require real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. All requests complete without tag failures. On a
fixed set of 300 redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B)
all produce 900/900 syntactically valid outputs with p95 latencies of
23, 18, and 31\,ms respectively.

Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation.
For each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Leave-dataset-out mapping quality. V-measure between
mapping-derived \texttt{phase} and native \texttt{action} labels.
13{,}265 operations from the four oracle-rich families
across 9 held-out evaluations.}
\label{tab:vmeasure}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Held-out dataset & Ops & V-measure & Boundary F1 \\
\midrule
mind2web & 774 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
webshop-expert & 2{,}504 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
swe-agent & 496 & 0.926 & 0.962 \\
weblinx-chat & 500 & 0.872 & 0.860 \\
agenttrek & 200 & 0.862 & --- \\
gui-odyssey & 7{,}868 & 0.811 & 0.842 \\
android-control & 9 & 0.716 & 0.727 \\
toolbench & 866 & 0.134 & 0.353 \\
api-bank & 48 & 0.000 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure
exceeds 0.7, indicating strong agreement between mapping-derived and
native labels. The two low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have
atypical action vocabularies that the held-out mapping rules do not
cover. Mapping reduces unique stacks on 6/9 datasets with zero negative
regressions.

A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
F1~1.0). These baseline comparisons support field derivation as a guarded configuration
step, not automatic intent discovery.

Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
on the same 13{,}265 operations and produce identical V-measure on 7/9
datasets, with the two divergent datasets differing by $\leq$0.17.
Mapping quality is robust to minor rule variations on well-covered
action vocabularies. Direct cross-backend comparison between the regex
and LLM taggers on the same free-form prompts remains future work.

Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set. The 3B model produces a broader
vocabulary (328 unique prompt labels) but includes noisy entries. A
deterministic alias pipeline reduces unique labels from 1{,}546 to
1{,}364, raising top-20 support coverage
from 93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw labels. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy. The ground-truth and
cross-backend checks above provide that.

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations), and all produce
identical output with median runtime 1.6\,s per spec.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Related Work}

Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage. Profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is structural. Pprof's tagroot adds label-derived frames to
an existing execution call stack. Agent traces have no execution stack,
so the entire profiling structure must be constructed from semantic
fields. The evaluation also differs: \toolname scores profiler output
against hidden agent-trajectory labels, a methodology with no analogue
in CPU profiling.

OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging. \toolname complements them with cross-session
aggregate profiling. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} and Laminar Signals~\cite{laminar-signals} take
steps toward semantic aggregation by clustering user messages or
extracting structured events, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions}, not \emph{resource attribution}.

AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas~\cite{agentatlas} argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying
which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most
budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions, operations and operation stacks, close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. Scoring profiler output against hidden trajectory labels confirms
that semantic profiling separates information that flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

Profilers and debuggers are complementary. Fixed-session drilldown finds
a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks (RQ2), while the profiler
identifies which categories deserve attention. \toolname supports both
by including or excluding session fields in the stack query. The
profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is designed
for automated consumption by analysis agents, though evaluation of
agent-driven diagnosis is future work.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data. Multi-project
evaluation and trace-ecosystem integration (importing OpenTelemetry and
LangSmith traces as operations) are the most impactful next steps.

**Should-fix. "deterministic alias pipeline" (l.681).** Invented compound — a reviewer would ask "what is that?" Replace with plain language: "a deterministic aliasing step" or "alias-based deduplication."

**Consider. "hidden-label localization" (l.128, l.540).** Invented compound used as a method name. It's self-explanatory and defined by the surrounding context (l.129–132 explains it). Borderline acceptable since it functions as a section/method label rather than unexplained jargon.

One sentence packing three claims. Could split after "merge" for readability.

Register is consistent throughout. No colloquial intrusions. ✓

# Paper Structure and Flow Check

Check a systems paper's structure at macro and micro levels. Report findings without editing.

## First Step

Read the paper. Determine the paper type by page count or venue:
- 12-14 pages → read `references/full-paper-12p.md`
- 6 pages → read `references/workshop-paper-6p.md` (inherits from full paper, lists only differences)
- 2 pages → read `references/extended-abstract-2p.md`

Then check at three levels.

## Level 1: Macro Structure

Compare the paper's section list against the template for its type. Check:
- Are all required sections present? Any missing?
- Is the ordering correct?
- Is Background separate from Motivation (full paper) or merged (workshop)?
- Does Design open with goals/requirements/principles + system overview?
- Does Design include an architecture diagram?
- Is Design separated from Implementation?
- Are subsections balanced in length?
- Is page budget roughly correct per section?

## Level 2: Paragraph Roles

For each section, check whether paragraphs play the correct roles as defined in the template. Focus especially on:

- **Abstract:** Does it follow the sentence-role structure? Correct word count? Does every abstract sentence map to an intro paragraph with the same claims, numbers, and terminology (no concept debuting in the abstract, no logic jumps)?
- **Introduction:** Are all required paragraph roles present (¶1 background, ¶2 problem, ¶4 existing solutions, ¶5 insight, ¶6 this paper, ¶7 contributions — never merged)? If ¶3 (root cause) is absent, is the cause still named at the end of ¶2 when ¶5's insight answers one? If ¶5b (challenges) is present, does ¶6 answer its challenges one-for-one? Does each paragraph's first sentence state that paragraph's topic? Are transitions at the start of new paragraphs, not the end of previous ones? Does ¶1 give background (not hook/problem)? Does ¶5 state the insight separately from the system?
- **Design:** Does it open with design goals? Is each subsection one design decision with why-before-what?
- **Evaluation:** Does each subsection correspond to a research question? Is there a setup paragraph?

## Level 2.5: Subsection Naming

Subsection titles must follow these conventions:
- **Noun phrases only.** Not questions ("Why X?"), not claims ("X Stops Y"), not verbs ("Implementing X").
- **Parallel structure within a section.** If one subsection is "Threat Model", siblings should be similar noun phrases ("Per-Tool Sandboxing", "Pipeline Composition"), not mixed styles.
- **Descriptive of content, not argument.** The title says what's IN the subsection, not what point it makes.
- **No "How" / "Why" / "What" question-style titles.**
- **No redundant system name.** Don't repeat the system name in every subsection title.

Bad: "Why Per-Tool Confinement", "How It Stops Attacks"
Good: "Motivation", "Per-Tool Sandboxing", "Pipeline Composition"

## Level 3: Paragraph-Internal Flow

For every paragraph:
- **Topic sentence first.** First sentence states what the paragraph is about.
- **One idea per paragraph.** Split if two distinct points.
- **Why before what.** Motivation before mechanism in design paragraphs.
- **Old-to-new.** Each sentence starts with known information, ends with new.
- **Logical connectors.** Paragraphs linked by transitions (cause, contrast, elaboration).

## Output Format

```
MACRO: [section-level issue]
MICRO: [paragraph-role issue]
FLOW:  [within-paragraph issue]
```

Prioritize as Must-fix / Should-fix / Consider.
