58	\label{sec:intro}
59	
60	%% ¶1: Background + Context
61	AI agents orchestrate heterogeneous activities: prompts, LLM calls,
62	tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
63	As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, developers need
64	cross-session aggregate views to
65	identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures
66	concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.
67	
68	%% ¶2: Problem + example
69	However, no existing tool provides cross-session resource attribution
70	by semantic category. In a real development project,
71	\texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times across 325 sessions, yet no
72	observability tool can attribute these executions to the review,
73	debugging, or refactoring prompts that triggered them. The same gap
74	affects failure and safety analysis: unsafe operations may cluster in
75	specific task phases, but no tool surfaces this without manual
76	inspection of individual sessions.
77	
78	%% ¶3: Root cause
79	The aggregation problem itself is not new: CPU profilers solved it for
80	programs decades ago.
81	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
82	into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
83	\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
84	Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
85	language, and two prompts expressing the same intent share no
86	characters (\S\ref{sec:background}).
87	
88	%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
89	Existing agent observability tools do not solve the aggregation problem.
90	LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
91	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
92	events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
93	not cross-session aggregation. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} clusters user messages
94	by topic, and Laminar~\cite{laminar-signals} extracts structured signals
95	from traces. Both
96	characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
97	questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
98	consume 40\% of the token budget''), because clustering at the request
99	level does not propagate labels to downstream system effects.
100	
101	%% ¶5: Key insight
102	We observe that three interdependent elements restore cross-session
103	aggregation for agent traces. A uniform \emph{operation} record that
104	spans both agent intent and system effects replaces the missing
105	call-stack sample. A query-time \emph{operation stack}
106	replaces the call stack with a field projection chosen at query time.
107	And \emph{intent recognition} restores the deterministic labels that
108	flame-graph folding requires.

140	\section{Background and Motivation}
141	\label{sec:background}
142	
143	\subsection{AI Agent Observability}
144	
145	AI agents orchestrate heterogeneous activities that span two layers:
146	high-level intent (prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations) and low-level
147	system effects (process spawns, file and network I/O). Existing
148	observability tools cover these layers separately.
149	LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
150	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
151	agent-level events into per-execution \emph{span trees}. System
152	monitors show process and file activity without semantic attribution.
153	The span-tree design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate
154	a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain.
155	AgentSight~\cite{agentsight} bridges the two layers by correlating
156	eBPF-captured system events with intercepted LLM traffic, but the
157	resulting traces still lack aggregate profiling.
158	
159	\subsection{Profiling vs.\ Debugging}
160	
161	Debugging inspects a single execution. Profiling aggregates across
162	executions to answer questions like ``where does the budget go?'' CPU
163	profilers solved this aggregation problem decades ago.
164	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as weighted
165	\emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack}. Identical stacks
166	merge, and width represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is
167	\emph{deterministic} function names: the same code path always produces
168	the same frames.
169	
170	Agent activities break this precondition in two ways. First, prompts
171	are natural language and lack deterministic identifiers. Second, there
172	is no inherent call stack: agent events have no runtime-determined
173	parent-child nesting analogous to function calls.
174	Pprof's \texttt{tagroot}/\texttt{tagleaf} options add label-derived
175	pseudo-frames to an existing execution stack, but agent activities have
176	no execution stack to augment.
177	
178	\subsection{The Aggregation Gap}
179	
180	Existing agent observability tools are designed for debugging, not
181	profiling, and this creates three concrete gaps.
182	
183	First, sessions are boundaries, not categories. A single session may
184	contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
185	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Two sessions performing
186	the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged without
187	external logic.
188	
189	Second, span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall},
190	\texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent
191	(\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name
192	tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work
193	consumed the budget.
194	
195	Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect
196	like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
197	but a flat summary shows only a single counter with no way to attribute
198	executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We quantify this
199	in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).
200	
201	These observations yield three design requirements:
202	
203	\begin{description}
204	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
205	  Agent activities mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI
206	  actions, process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a
207	  single record type that can represent all of them without
208	  type-specific objects.
209	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
210	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
211	  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the input.
212	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
213	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
214	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
215	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
216	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
217	\end{description}
218

220	\section{Design}
221	\label{sec:design}
222	
223	The three requirements (a uniform record type, query-time aggregation,
224	and deterministic labels for folding) drive the design. The profiling
225	pipeline has five stages: (1)~parse raw traces into operations,
226	(2)~label operations via intent recognition or mapping rules,
227	(3)~filter by a user-specified predicate, (4)~project each operation
228	onto a stack frame sequence chosen at query time, and (5)~fold
229	operations with identical stacks, summing their weights. We introduce
230	two abstractions that satisfy R1 and R2, operations
231	(\S\ref{sec:ops}) and operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks}), and a
232	pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
233	satisfies R3.
234	
235	\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
236	\label{sec:ops}
237	
238	Agent activities span two layers: high-level intent (prompts, LLM
239	calls, tool invocations) and the system effects they trigger (process
240	spawns, file reads, network requests). A profiler should not
241	distinguish between these layers at the object-model level. \toolname
242	uses a single abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with
243	string fields and additive measures.
244	
245	Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
246	\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
247	\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
248	measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
249	call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
250	are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
251	
252	\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
253	\label{sec:stacks}
254	
255	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time.
256	Given a stack specification $[f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_k]$, each operation
257	$o$ is projected to a frame sequence $\langle o.f_1, o.f_2, \ldots,
258	o.f_k \rangle$. Operations with identical frame sequences are merged
259	and their weights are summed. The result is the standard folded-stack
260	representation:
261	
262	\begin{small}
263	\begin{verbatim}
264	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
265	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
266	\end{verbatim}
267	\end{small}
268	
269	\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
270	execution, the stack is determined by the query. The same
271	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
272	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
273	Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
274	Failure, safety, and quality labels are ordinary fields that
275	participate in the same projection, so the profiler handles diagnostic
276	views without a separate mechanism.
277	
278	Query-time stack selection directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem
279	from \S\ref{sec:background}. Sessions and spans are optional operation
280	fields,
281	not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
282	produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree). Excluding
283	it produces an aggregate view that existing trace tools do not
284	natively support. The same data supports both debugging and profiling
285	views.
286	
287	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate
288	$\varphi$ selects which operations participate, a stack function
289	$\sigma = [f_1, \ldots, f_k]$ maps each operation to its frame
290	sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
291	views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
292	questions.

322	\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
323	\label{sec:intent}
324	
325	Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
326	folding still requires deterministic frame labels, the precondition
327	that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
328	this by mapping free-form prompts to
329	short, stable labels before stack construction.
330	
331	The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends.
332	First, \emph{regex rules} are the production default. Rules have the
333	form \texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
334	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
335	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
336	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: the developer
337	runs \toolname, observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds
338	rules, re-runs, and iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This
339	typically takes 5--10 rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic,
340	reproducible, and version-controllable.
341	Second, a \emph{local LLM tagger} handles exploration or complex
342	multilingual prompts. A local model (e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via
343	llama.cpp) generates a single-word label per prompt.
344	Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity. Labels are
345	cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
346	Third, \emph{unsupervised clustering} via TF-IDF vectorization and
347	K-Means discovers natural prompt groups without predefined rules,
348	feeding rule authoring.
349	
350	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
351	short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
352	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
353	
354	For structured traces such as public benchmark datasets, where action
355	types, tool names, and quality annotations are explicit fields, intent
356	recognition is unnecessary. \toolname supports deterministic
357	\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing
358	ones before stack construction. For example, the rule
359	\texttt{phase:navigate=type:(click|scroll|key)} maps raw action types
360	to a coarser \texttt{phase} field, enabling cross-dataset aggregation
361	without modifying the input.
362	
363	The intent-recognition and mapping-rule paths are both pluggable. New
364	backends (e.g., embedding-based classifiers, external LLM APIs, or
365	domain-specific heuristics) can be added without changing the
366	operation or stack abstractions. A \emph{profile spec} records the
367	complete analysis configuration (data sources, backend choice, mappings,
368	predicates, stack fields, and outputs) for deterministic replay. Both
369	paths produce operations with fields, and the stack query works
370	identically on both.

373	\section{Implementation}
374	\label{sec:impl}
375	
376	\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler implemented as a Rust CLI
377	(Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). It reads recorded traces, not live
378	events. The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
379	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
380	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
381	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
382	semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
383	instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
384	mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
385	Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
386	fields preserved as operation fields.
387	
388	Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
389	\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
390	\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
391	All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.
392	
393	\toolname is the offline profiling component of the broader
394	AgentSight~\cite{agentsight} observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
395	capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects.
396	\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
397	are complementary. AgentSight answers ``what happened during this run''
398	(debugging), \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across runs''
399	(profiling).

716	%% ===================================================================
717	\section{Related Work}
718	
719	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
720	folded-stack lineage. Profiles are weighted samples with location
721	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
722	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
723	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
724	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
725	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
726	difference is structural. Pprof's tagroot adds label-derived frames to
727	an existing execution call stack. Agent traces have no execution stack,
728	so the entire profiling structure must be constructed from semantic
729	fields. The evaluation also differs: \toolname scores profiler output
730	against hidden agent-trajectory labels, a methodology with no analogue
731	in CPU profiling.
732	
733	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
734	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
735	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
736	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
737	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
738	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts.
739	AgentTelemetry~\cite{agenttelemetry} defines 14 fault types over 9
740	agent-specific span kinds that extend OpenTelemetry for agent
741	orchestration phases. Wang et al.~\cite{agenttraces-trust} survey
742	evidence tracing and execution provenance as foundations for agent
743	accountability. These systems excel at single-execution debugging or
744	fault detection. \toolname complements them with cross-session aggregate
745	profiling. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} and Laminar
746	Signals~\cite{laminar-signals} take steps toward semantic aggregation by
747	clustering user messages or extracting structured events, but they
748	characterize \emph{input distributions}, not \emph{resource
749	attribution}.
750	
751	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
752	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
753	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
754	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas~\cite{agentatlas} argues that
755	outcome leaderboards miss trajectory-level quality.
756	TrajAD~\cite{trajad} and AgentFixer~\cite{agentfixer} detect trajectory
757	anomalies and recommend fixes. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
758	or \emph{step-level} fault localization within a single execution.
759	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying
760	which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most
761	budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions.
762	
763	%% ===================================================================
764	\section{Conclusion}
765	
766	
767	Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. \toolname
768	shows that two abstractions, operations and operation stacks, close the
769	aggregation problem once intent recognition restores deterministic labels.
770	Scoring profiler output against hidden trajectory labels confirms that
771	semantic profiling separates over 90\% of mixed system-effect weight,
772	localizes labeled problems at 9.4\% inspection cost versus flat
773	summaries, and produces labels that agree with ground truth on 7/9
774	held-out datasets. Fixed-session drilldown remains faster to a first
775	positive on 4/6 tasks, confirming that profilers and debuggers are
776	complementary, and \toolname supports both by including or excluding
777	session fields in the stack query. The main limitations are
778	single-project real-session data and placeholder intent-recognition
779	quality on free-form prompts. Multi-project evaluation and
780	trace-ecosystem integration are the most impactful next steps.

\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agents}

\begin{abstract}
AI agents orchestrate heterogeneous activities (prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects). As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, developers need aggregate
views to identify which task categories consume the most budget, where
failures concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.
Yet, existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. The consequence is that
failures, safety violations, and wasted effort remain unattributable to
the task categories that cause them.
The root cause is structural: agent prompts are natural language, so
two prompts with the same intent share no identifiers that a profiler
could merge.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions (uniform
\emph{operations} spanning agent intent and system effects, and
query-time \emph{operation stacks}) once intent
recognition restores the deterministic labels that flame-graph folding
requires.
\toolname implements this model as a Rust profiler with pluggable
intent-recognition backends.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate over 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels (34{,}539 operations), operation-stack
profiling reduces inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and
group fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agents orchestrate heterogeneous activities: prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions, developers need
cross-session aggregate views to
identify which task categories consume the most budget, where failures
concentrate, and which workflows waste effort.

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, no existing tool provides cross-session resource attribution
by semantic category. In a real development project,
\texttt{cargo test} appears 2{,}903 times across 325 sessions, yet no
observability tool can attribute these executions to the review,
debugging, or refactoring prompts that triggered them. The same gap
affects failure and safety analysis: unsafe operations may cluster in
specific task phases, but no tool surfaces this without manual
inspection of individual sessions.

%% ¶3: Root cause
The aggregation problem itself is not new: CPU profilers solved it for
programs decades ago.
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition because prompts are natural
language, and two prompts expressing the same intent share no
characters (\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Existing agent observability tools do not solve the aggregation problem.
LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
events into per-execution span trees, enabling single-run debugging but
not cross-session aggregation. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} clusters user messages
by topic, and Laminar~\cite{laminar-signals} extracts structured signals
from traces. Both
characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget''), because clustering at the request
level does not propagate labels to downstream system effects.

%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that three interdependent elements restore cross-session
aggregation for agent traces. A uniform \emph{operation} record that
spans both agent intent and system effects replaces the missing
call-stack sample. A query-time \emph{operation stack}
replaces the call stack with a field projection chosen at query time.
And \emph{intent recognition} restores the deterministic labels that
flame-graph folding requires.

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a Rust profiler built on this model.
On 325 real Codex/Claude sessions, semantic labels separate over 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
with hidden ground-truth labels, operation-stack profiling reduces
inspection work to 9.4\% versus flat summaries and group fragmentation
by 45\% versus fixed-session drilldown.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A two-abstraction profiling model} that defines a
  uniform operation record spanning agent intent and system effects,
  a query-time operation stack,
  and an intent-recognition step for restoring deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  A profiler that realizes this model with pluggable intent recognition
  (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
  produces output (pprof, SVG, JSON) consumable by both developers and
  automated analysis agents (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation via hidden-label localization.}
  We score profiler output against hidden ground-truth trajectory
  labels (failure, safety, redundancy, and human-task boundaries),
  analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler evaluation
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{AI Agent Observability}

AI agents orchestrate heterogeneous activities that span two layers:
high-level intent (prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations) and low-level
system effects (process spawns, file and network I/O). Existing
observability tools cover these layers separately.
LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel} organize
agent-level events into per-execution \emph{span trees}. System
monitors show process and file activity without semantic attribution.
The span-tree design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate
a failing span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain.
AgentSight~\cite{agentsight} bridges the two layers by correlating
eBPF-captured system events with intercepted LLM traffic, but the
resulting traces still lack aggregate profiling.

\subsection{Profiling vs.\ Debugging}

Debugging inspects a single execution. Profiling aggregates across
executions to answer questions like ``where does the budget go?'' CPU
profilers solved this aggregation problem decades ago.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as weighted
\emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack}. Identical stacks
merge, and width represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names: the same code path always produces
the same frames.

Agent activities break this precondition in two ways. First, prompts
are natural language and lack deterministic identifiers. Second, there
is no inherent call stack: agent events have no runtime-determined
parent-child nesting analogous to function calls.
Pprof's \texttt{tagroot}/\texttt{tagleaf} options add label-derived
pseudo-frames to an existing execution stack, but agent activities have
no execution stack to augment.

\subsection{The Aggregation Gap}

Existing agent observability tools are designed for debugging, not
profiling, and this creates three concrete gaps.

First, sessions are boundaries, not categories. A single session may
contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Two sessions performing
the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged without
external logic.

Second, span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall},
\texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent
(\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name
tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work
consumed the budget.

Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect
like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
but a flat summary shows only a single counter with no way to attribute
executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We quantify this
in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent activities mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI
  actions, process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a
  single record type that can represent all of them without
  type-specific objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes (by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset) without rebuilding the input.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements (a uniform record type, query-time aggregation,
and deterministic labels for folding) drive the design. The profiling
pipeline has five stages: (1)~parse raw traces into operations,
(2)~label operations via intent recognition or mapping rules,
(3)~filter by a user-specified predicate, (4)~project each operation
onto a stack frame sequence chosen at query time, and (5)~fold
operations with identical stacks, summing their weights. We introduce
two abstractions that satisfy R1 and R2, operations
(\S\ref{sec:ops}) and operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks}), and a
pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
satisfies R3.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
\label{sec:ops}

Agent activities span two layers: high-level intent (prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations) and the system effects they trigger (process
spawns, file reads, network requests). A profiler should not
distinguish between these layers at the object-model level. \toolname
uses a single abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with
string fields and additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time.
Given a stack specification $[f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_k]$, each operation
$o$ is projected to a frame sequence $\langle o.f_1, o.f_2, \ldots,
o.f_k \rangle$. Operations with identical frame sequences are merged
and their weights are summed. The result is the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
Failure, safety, and quality labels are ordinary fields that
participate in the same projection, so the profiler handles diagnostic
views without a separate mechanism.

Query-time stack selection directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem
from \S\ref{sec:background}. Sessions and spans are optional operation
fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree). Excluding
it produces an aggregate view that existing trace tools do not
natively support. The same data supports both debugging and profiling
views.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate
$\varphi$ selects which operations participate, a stack function
$\sigma = [f_1, \ldots, f_k]$ maps each operation to its frame
sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
questions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{figures/fig-architecture.tex}}
\caption{System architecture. Local agent histories enter through
\texttt{agent-session} parsing. Public datasets enter as operation JSONL.
Both paths produce operations. The stack query and output are identical.}
\Description{Data flow from agent traces through parsing and intent
recognition to folded-stack flame graphs.}
\label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels, the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this by mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends.
First, \emph{regex rules} are the production default. Rules have the
form \texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: the developer
runs \toolname, observes the unmatched rate and sample prompts, adds
rules, re-runs, and iterates until unmatched drops below 5\%. This
typically takes 5--10 rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic,
reproducible, and version-controllable.
Second, a \emph{local LLM tagger} handles exploration or complex
multilingual prompts. A local model (e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via
llama.cpp) generates a single-word label per prompt.
Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity. Labels are
cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
Third, \emph{unsupervised clustering} via TF-IDF vectorization and
K-Means discovers natural prompt groups without predefined rules,
feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

For structured traces such as public benchmark datasets, where action
types, tool names, and quality annotations are explicit fields, intent
recognition is unnecessary. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing
ones before stack construction. For example, the rule
\texttt{phase:navigate=type:(click|scroll|key)} maps raw action types
to a coarser \texttt{phase} field, enabling cross-dataset aggregation
without modifying the input.

The intent-recognition and mapping-rule paths are both pluggable. New
backends (e.g., embedding-based classifiers, external LLM APIs, or
domain-specific heuristics) can be added without changing the
operation or stack abstractions. A \emph{profile spec} records the
complete analysis configuration (data sources, backend choice, mappings,
predicates, stack fields, and outputs) for deterministic replay. Both
paths produce operations with fields, and the stack query works
identically on both.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler implemented as a Rust CLI
(Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). It reads recorded traces, not live
events. The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
fields preserved as operation fields.

Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.

\toolname is the offline profiling component of the broader
AgentSight~\cite{agentsight} observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects.
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
are complementary. AgentSight answers ``what happened during this run''
(debugging), \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across runs''
(profiling).

%% ===================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2.
We measure semantic separation (mixed-weight percentage), localization
quality (AP, recall, work-to-first-positive), and label agreement
(V-measure, boundary F1).

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling (aggregation
by intent-derived labels) is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets (those containing observations from
multiple semantic regions) under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets. A flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles, $p = 0.001$) confirms the
separation is not random. Label quality is validated in RQ3.

RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
objects, validating R1. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
stack fields. A flat GROUP BY on a single label cannot produce these views because
different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens.

Figure~\ref{fig:rq1-separation} visualizes the ablation.
Figures~\ref{fig:flamegraph} and~\ref{fig:flamegraph-files} show
the resulting flame graphs for the \texttt{tokens} and \texttt{files}
views respectively: changing only the stack fields and weight function
produces different aggregates from the same operations.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig-rq1-separation.pdf}
\caption{RQ1: Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations.
Adding prompt labels reduces mixed weight from 90.4\% to 36.7\%.
Session labels alone barely help (84.4\%).}
\Description{Stacked bar chart showing mixed vs separated weight
under four projection choices.}
\label{fig:rq1-separation}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
\caption{Flame graph of the \texttt{tokens} view across 325 real
sessions. Width represents token count. The bottom frames show project
and agent; middle frames show sessions and prompt labels
(\texttt{continue}, \texttt{query}, \texttt{review}, \texttt{design});
top frames show individual LLM calls and models. The same data produces
different views by changing the stack fields
(Table~\ref{tab:views}).}
\Description{Wide flame graph showing token budget distribution across
sessions, prompt categories, and LLM models.}
\label{fig:flamegraph}
\end{figure*}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering

\Description{Wide flame graph showing file-access distribution across

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

RQ2 asks whether the profiler's top groups correspond to real labeled
problems, specifically whether categories that concentrate failures, safety
violations, or wasted effort surface at the top of ranked output. The
methodology is analogous to injecting known
bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation. Public benchmark datasets
provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
positives.

The benchmark uses six tasks across four datasets (AgentRewardBench
looping and side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect
and redundant step, and OSWorld-Human group start), totaling 34{,}539 operations and
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.
``---'' = group count varies by task; no single median is reported.}
\label{tab:localization}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
\midrule
flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

Figure~\ref{fig:rq2-tradeoff} visualizes this tradeoff: op-stack
query-aware sits in the low-work, moderate-recall region. The comparison also
serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (\S\ref{sec:design}). Fixed-session
drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
tasks, confirming that profilers and debuggers are complementary.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/baseline-tradeoff.png}
\caption{RQ2: Inspection work vs.\ budget-30 recall across policies.
Op-stack query-aware (labeled) achieves low work (0.094) with moderate
recall (0.39), while flat requires full inspection and fixed-session
fragments into 285 groups. Oracle policies (large dots) are upper bounds.}
\Description{Scatter plot showing inspection work versus budget recall
for eight profiling policies.}
\label{fig:rq2-tradeoff}
\end{figure}

Statistical validation supports these comparisons. Bootstrap
(10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials) confirm
stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\% prevalence/group-size null on all
six tasks.

Beyond localization, we test whether profiler output suggests concrete
configuration improvements. Executable profile-spec patches modify
stack fields, mapping rules, or rankers, then re-run over the same
visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from stack-based
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives. Folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Are the Derived Labels?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level. Quality
assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
remains future work.

On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
with zero failures and p95 latency of 31\,ms per label.

Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation.
For each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Leave-dataset-out mapping quality. V-measure between
mapping-derived \texttt{phase} and native \texttt{action} labels.
13{,}265 operations from the four oracle-rich families
across 9 held-out evaluations.}
\label{tab:vmeasure}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Held-out dataset & Ops & V-measure & Boundary F1 \\
\midrule
mind2web & 774 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
webshop-expert & 2{,}504 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
swe-agent & 496 & 0.926 & 0.962 \\
weblinx-chat & 500 & 0.872 & 0.860 \\
agenttrek & 200 & 0.862 & --- \\
gui-odyssey & 7{,}868 & 0.811 & 0.842 \\
android-control & 9 & 0.716 & 0.727 \\
toolbench & 866 & 0.134 & 0.353 \\
api-bank & 48 & 0.000 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig-rq3-vmeasure.pdf}
\caption{RQ3: Leave-dataset-out V-measure between mapping-derived
\texttt{phase} and native \texttt{action} labels. The dashed line
marks 0.7. Seven of nine datasets exceed this threshold.}
\Description{Bar chart showing V-measure for nine held-out datasets,
with a dashed line at 0.7.}
\label{fig:rq3-vmeasure}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} and Figure~\ref{fig:rq3-vmeasure} show the
results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure exceeds 0.7, indicating strong
agreement between mapping-derived and native labels. The two
low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have atypical action
vocabularies that the held-out mapping rules do not cover.

A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
F1~1.0). These baseline comparisons support field derivation as a guarded configuration
step, not automatic intent discovery.

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations), and all produce
identical output with median runtime 1.6\,s per spec.

\section{Related Work}

Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage. Profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is structural. Pprof's tagroot adds label-derived frames to
an existing execution call stack. Agent traces have no execution stack,
so the entire profiling structure must be constructed from semantic
fields. The evaluation also differs: \toolname scores profiler output
against hidden agent-trajectory labels, a methodology with no analogue
in CPU profiling.

OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts.
AgentTelemetry~\cite{agenttelemetry} defines 14 fault types over 9
agent-specific span kinds that extend OpenTelemetry for agent
orchestration phases. Wang et al.~\cite{agenttraces-trust} survey
evidence tracing and execution provenance as foundations for agent
accountability. These systems excel at single-execution debugging or
fault detection. \toolname complements them with cross-session aggregate
profiling. Datadog LLM Observability~\cite{datadog-llmobs} and Laminar
Signals~\cite{laminar-signals} take steps toward semantic aggregation by
clustering user messages or extracting structured events, but they
characterize \emph{input distributions}, not \emph{resource
attribution}.

AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas~\cite{agentatlas} argues that
outcome leaderboards miss trajectory-level quality.
TrajAD~\cite{trajad} and AgentFixer~\cite{agentfixer} detect trajectory
anomalies and recommend fixes. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
or \emph{step-level} fault localization within a single execution.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying
which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most
budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}


Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. \toolname
shows that two abstractions, operations and operation stacks, close the
aggregation problem once intent recognition restores deterministic labels.
Scoring profiler output against hidden trajectory labels confirms that
semantic profiling separates over 90\% of mixed system-effect weight,
localizes labeled problems at 9.4\% inspection cost versus flat
summaries, and produces labels that agree with ground truth on 7/9
held-out datasets. Fixed-session drilldown remains faster to a first
positive on 4/6 tasks, confirming that profilers and debuggers are
complementary, and \toolname supports both by including or excluding
session fields in the stack query. The main limitations are
single-project real-session data and placeholder intent-recognition
quality on free-form prompts. Multi-project evaluation and
trace-ecosystem integration are the most impactful next steps.

# LaTeX Bilingual Format

Convert a LaTeX paper so that every English sentence is on its own line, followed by a `% 中文翻译。` comment on the next line.

## Format

```latex
English sentence here.
% 中文翻译在这里。
Next English sentence.
% 下一句中文翻译。
```

## Rules

1. **One English sentence per line.** Split paragraphs into individual sentences.
2. **Chinese translation comment immediately after.** Every English sentence gets a `%` comment with its Chinese translation on the next line.
3. **Do NOT change any English text.** Only reformat line breaks and add `%` comments.
4. **Preserve all LaTeX commands.** Labels, refs, citations, macros, environments — all stay intact.
5. **Skip these environments** — leave them as-is, do not add Chinese:
   - `\begin{table}` ... `\end{table}` (including tabular content)
   - `\begin{figure}` ... `\end{figure}`
   - `\begin{lstlisting}` ... `\end{lstlisting}`
   - `\begin{CCSXML}` ... `\end{CCSXML}`
   - `\begin{itemize}` items — add Chinese after each `\item` line
6. **Section/subsection headers** — add Chinese comment after the header line.
7. **Existing Chinese comments** — replace with new per-sentence translations if the format doesn't match (e.g., old paragraph-level comments).
8. **Figure/table captions** — add Chinese comment after the caption line.

## Process

Work section by section, top to bottom:
1. Abstract
2. Introduction
3. Background and Motivation
4. Design
5. Implementation
6. Evaluation
7. Related Work
8. Conclusion

After each section, compile (`make` or `latexmk`) to verify the output is unchanged (same page count, no errors). The Chinese comments should not affect compilation.

## Translation Quality

- Use natural Chinese, not word-by-word translation
- Technical terms: keep the English term on first use, e.g., "沙箱 (sandbox)"
- System names: keep English (Sandlock, Docker, Landlock)
- Acronyms: keep English (MCP, API, SSH)
- Be concise — the Chinese should be shorter than or equal to the English

Base directory for this skill: /home/yunwei37/.claude/skills/latex-bilingual-format

# LaTeX Bilingual Format

Convert a LaTeX paper so that every English sentence is on its own line, followed by a `% 中文翻译。` comment on the next line.

## Format

```latex
English sentence here.
% 中文翻译在这里。
Next English sentence.
% 下一句中文翻译。
```

## Rules

1. **One English sentence per line.** Split paragraphs into individual sentences.
2. **Chinese translation comment immediately after.** Every English sentence gets a `%` comment with its Chinese translation on the next line.
3. **Do NOT change any English text.** Only reformat line breaks and add `%` comments.
4. **Preserve all LaTeX commands.** Labels, refs, citations, macros, environments — all stay intact.
5. **Skip these environments** — leave them as-is, do not add Chinese:
   - `\begin{table}` ... `\end{table}` (including tabular content)
   - `\begin{figure}` ... `\end{figure}`
   - `\begin{lstlisting}` ... `\end{lstlisting}`
   - `\begin{CCSXML}` ... `\end{CCSXML}`
   - `\begin{itemize}` items — add Chinese after each `\item` line
6. **Section/subsection headers** — add Chinese comment after the header line.
7. **Existing Chinese comments** — replace with new per-sentence translations if the format doesn't match (e.g., old paragraph-level comments).
8. **Figure/table captions** — add Chinese comment after the caption line.

## Process

Work section by section, top to bottom:
1. Abstract
2. Introduction
3. Background and Motivation
4. Design
5. Implementation
6. Evaluation
7. Related Work
8. Conclusion

After each section, compile (`make` or `latexmk`) to verify the output is unchanged (same page count, no errors). The Chinese comments should not affect compilation.

## Translation Quality

- Use natural Chinese, not word-by-word translation
- Technical terms: keep the English term on first use, e.g., "沙箱 (sandbox)"
- System names: keep English (Sandlock, Docker, Landlock)
- Acronyms: keep English (MCP, API, SSH)
- Be concise — the Chinese should be shorter than or equal to the English

skills.name: paper-writing-style
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/yunwei37/.claude/skills/paper-writing-style

# Academic Paper Writing Review & Fix

Review the LaTeX file at `` sentence by sentence for academic writing quality. If no argument is given, ask which section to review.

## Review process

1. Read the entire file
2. Check terminology consistency (Section T below) FIRST
3. For each paragraph, analyze every sentence against the checklist below
4. Report issues grouped by severity: **Must fix** (clarity/logic errors), **Should fix** (antipatterns), **Consider** (style preferences)
5. For each issue, give the line number, quote the problematic text, explain the problem, and suggest a concrete rewrite
6. Apply the fixes directly with the Edit tool — Must fix first, then Should fix, then evaluate each Consider item and apply the ones that improve the text (note rejected ones with a one-line reason). Do not ask the user which fixes to apply, and do not silently discard anything below Must fix. Exception: when invoked read-only as a review subagent (e.g. from iter-refine-writing), report findings only and make no edits — the calling agent applies them.

## Editing discipline

- **Minimal targeted changes only** — never rewrite, restructure, or delete existing content unless explicitly asked.
- **When updating numbers/data, do NOT touch prose wording.**
- **Preserve the user's exact wording and meaning.** Do not soften, strengthen, or "fix grammar" unless asked; flag suggestions instead of applying them.
- **Avoid absolutist words** like "cannot", "impossible", "never" unless structurally true.
- **Do not invent non-standard terms.**
- **Deep pass on first attempt** — do thorough review (not just mechanical/surface fixes). Shallow first passes waste user time.
- **Verify before claiming done** — recompile LaTeX, check it builds. Do not claim "fixed" until verified.

## Critical rules (for fixes)

- **NEVER delete design decisions or technical content.** Compression means better prose, not less information.
- **NEVER change the meaning** of a sentence. If unsure, ask.
- **NEVER remove a scope-bearing hedge** (`suggest ... on the selected subset`, `in our setting`, `up to`): it protects the claim from outrunning its evidence . Only collapse stacked hedges down to one.
- **Always diff-check** after multiple edits to ensure no content was lost.
- **No em-dashes** (`---`) in paper text. Table `---` for N/A is fine.
- **No semicolons** joining independent clauses. Use periods, conjunctions, or causal connectors.
- **Why before what**: every design decision states its motivation first.
- **Example before abstraction**: show a concrete case, then generalize.
- **Subject first**: start important sentences with a concrete actor or object. Prefer "The profiler ranks...", "Operation stacks group...", or "The replay check verifies..." over vague starts like "This shows...", "These checks...", or note labels like "RQ setup". If the sentence reports evidence, name the thing being evaluated before naming the run, table, script, or artifact.
- **Use explicit author subjects when appropriate**: when the paper describes author choices or measurements, prefer "We compare...", "We evaluate...", "We treat labels as hidden oracles...", or "We find..." over agentless passive voice. When the sentence describes mechanism behavior, make the system or abstraction the subject: "The profiler ranks...", "The operation stack groups...", or "The mapper compresses...".
- **Claim before run history**: paper text must not read as a sequence of run IDs, scripts, gates, artifacts, or generated tables. Rewrite those into the claim being tested, the comparison, the result, and the limitation.
- **Paper, not project report**: reject prose that reads like a status update, experiment diary, artifact index, TODO list, README feature list, benchmark appendix, or terminology glossary. A paper section should tell the reader what claim matters and why the evidence supports or limits it.
- **Few substantial experiments**: evaluation prose should be organized around a small number of claim-facing research questions, usually 3-4 for a full paper, not many small script-shaped experiments.
- **No internal process vocabulary in main prose**: avoid gate, artifact ledger, run ledger, source-status, hygiene, generated-output, and reviewer packet unless the section is explicitly about reproducibility logistics.
- **Reproducibility is not another accuracy experiment**: replay, build, and scope-control sections should say what can be reproduced and which claims are bounded. They should not sound like they revalidate fidelity, actionability, or baseline superiority.

---

## Section T: Terminology Consistency (check FIRST)

Terminology problems confuse readers more than awkward prose. Run these checks before sentence-level review.

### T0: Unnecessary terms (P0)

Every introduced term must earn its keep. If a term adds reader burden without adding precision, remove it.

**Red flags**:
- Term defined but used only 1-2 times (inline the definition instead)
- Near-synonym of an existing term without clear distinction
- Jargon where plain language would work ("utilize" vs "use")
- Term that requires forward reference to understand current paragraph

**Test**: can a reader understand this paragraph without knowing this term? If yes, the term may be unnecessary.

### T1: Defined-before-used (P0)

Every technical term, acronym, and notation must be defined before first use, including in figure captions and table headers (readers hit these out of order).

**Check method**: for each technical term, find its definition location and first use location. If first use comes before definition, it's a P0 finding.

Common violations:
- Acronym used in abstract but only expanded in body
- Term in figure caption defined two subsections later
- Notation in table header explained at end of different subsection

### T2: Same concept, same term

Grep for near-synonyms. If the same concept uses multiple terms, unify to one.

```bash
grep -oE '(policy|rule|constraint|directive)' file.tex | sort | uniq -c
```

Common drift pairs to check:
- policy / rule / constraint / directive
- harness / runtime / framework
- enforce / check / validate / verify
- block / deny / prevent / reject

### T3: Compound adjective hyphenation

Compound adjectives before nouns need hyphens; standalone uses do not.

| Context | Correct | Wrong |
|---------|---------|-------|
| Before noun | tool-call guardrails | tool call guardrails |
| After verb | operates at the OS level | operates at the OS-level |
| Before noun | cross-event policy | cross event policy |

Check common compounds:
```bash
grep -oE '(tool|cross|per|intent|system|application|kernel)[- ](call|event|level)' file.tex | sort | uniq -c
```

### T4: Redundant `*-level` qualifiers

Many `*-level` compounds are redundant. Check if removing `-level` loses meaning:

| Often redundant | Usually needed |
|-----------------|----------------|
| system-level (just "system") | OS-level (vs tool-level) |
| kernel-level (just "kernel") | intent-level (vs syscall-level) |
| application-level (just "application") | enforcement-level (classification) |

Test: "system actions" vs "system-level actions" — if both mean the same, drop `-level`.

### T5: Capitalization consistency

Check proper nouns and acronyms:
```bash
grep -oE '(eBPF|EBPF|ebpf|BPF)' file.tex | sort | uniq -c
```

Common issues:
- eBPF (not EBPF, ebpf)
- GitHub (not Github, github)
- macOS (not MacOS, macos)

### T6: Spelling variants

Pick one and stick to it:
- runtime vs run-time
- pre-defined vs predefined
- sub-agent vs subagent

### T7: Invented terms (P0)

AI drafting tends to coin compound nouns that sound professional but do not exist in the field: "trusted obligation", "reference C/libbpf workflow", "production datapath", "artifact evaluation" appearing out of nowhere. Every non-standard term must be either (a) established usage in the target community, or (b) formally introduced by this paper with a definition at first use.

**Check method**: for each compound technical noun, ask "would a domain reviewer recognize this term, or did we invent it?" If invented and not deliberately introduced as a contribution, replace with plain language or the field's standard term.

**Red flags**:
- Compound noun appears exactly once, capitalized or hyphenated like a term of art, with no definition
- Term cannot be found in the paper's own related work or the field's standard literature
- Reader would ask "X 是啥?" — if the authors cannot answer in one sentence, delete the term

---

## Sentence-level antipatterns

### Semicolons joining independent clauses
Semicolons that join two independent clauses should be rewritten as:
- Two sentences (period)
- One sentence with a conjunction (", and", ", but", ", so")
- One sentence with a causal connector ("because", "since", "therefore")
Semicolons ARE acceptable inside parenthetical lists.

**Bad:** `The engine propagates labels; rules fire at each event.`
**Good:** `The engine propagates labels, and rules fire at each event.`
**Good:** `Because the engine propagates labels, rules fire at each event.`

### No bullet points or lists in narrative prose
Bullet points and enumerated lists are forbidden in narrative prose. They read like notes, not academic writing. Convert lists to flowing paragraphs with causal connectors.

**Exceptions (where lists ARE allowed):**
- Contribution lists in introduction (e.g., "We make three contributions:")
- Algorithm pseudocode or formal specifications
- Feature/capability tables comparing systems
- Explicit enumerations that will be referenced later ("Step 3 of the pipeline...")

**Bad (list in narrative):**
```
The optimization has four benefits:
\begin{itemize}
\item Reduces latency
\item Improves throughput
\item Lowers memory usage
\item Simplifies debugging
\end{itemize}
```

**Good (flowing prose):**
`The optimization reduces latency and improves throughput by eliminating redundant copies, while also lowering memory usage and simplifying debugging through a unified code path.`

### Note-like prose (short declarative sentences strung together)
Academic prose uses causal connectors, subordinate clauses, and flowing sentences. Short declarative sentences read like bullet points, not a paper.

**Bad:** `Labels propagate at fork. The child inherits the parent mask. Rules check the mask at each event.`
**Good:** `Labels propagate at fork, so the child inherits the parent mask and rules can check it at each event.`

Tie-breaker: this rule targets runs of three or more short declaratives. A pair of sentences produced by splitting an overlong sentence (e.g., to fix subject-verb separation) is fine — do not re-merge it.

### Narrative flow (tell a story, not notes)

Each paragraph should follow: **problem → idea → evidence**. Lead with the insight; numbers support it. The reader should know *why the data matters* before seeing the data.

**Bad (data dump):**
`217 (36\%) have one clause. 231 (38\%) have two. Policies average 71 tokens.`

**Good (narrative):**
`Most policies are structurally simple, making them amenable to agent generation: 74\% have at most two clauses, and the 95th percentile stays under 152 tokens.`

This applies especially to evaluation sections. State what the numbers mean, then give the numbers.

### Missing "why" before "what"
Every design decision must explain its motivation before describing the mechanism. Readers need to understand the problem before the solution.

**Bad:** `We use monotonic labels. Labels are never removed once added.`
**Good:** `To ensure no history is lost across the session, labels are monotonic: propagation adds labels but never removes them.`

### Em-dashes (---)
Never use em-dashes in paper text. Use commas, parentheses, semicolons (in lists), or restructure the sentence. Table cells using `---` for "not applicable" are acceptable.

### Colons (avoid unless introducing a numbered list)
**Default to avoiding colons.** Only use them for:
1. Introducing a **numbered list** with explicit markers like (1), (2), (3)

Never use colons for unlabeled lists, `claim: evidence`, `setup: result`, or `observation: explanation` patterns. These create note-like prose. Instead use causal connectors ("because", "so", "since"), conjunctions (", and"), or split into two sentences.

**Bad:** `Tool-call guardrails are insufficient: 83% of policies constrain system actions.` (claim: evidence)
**Bad:** `The engine uses eBPF: the verifier imposes a stack limit.` (setup: constraint)
**Bad:** `Optimization spans three layers: source, LLVM, and JIT.` (unlabeled list)
**Good:** `Tool-call guardrails are insufficient because 83% of policies constrain system actions.`
**Good:** `The framework addresses three goals: (1) crash isolation, (2) bounded action spaces, and (3) multi-layer feedback.` (numbered list)

## Word-level antipatterns

| Antipattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| "in order to" | "to" |
| "utilize" / "utilization" | "use" |
| "it is important to note that" | delete or rephrase |
| "it should be noted that" | delete or rephrase |
| "there is/are ... that" | rewrite with real subject |
| "due to the fact that" | "because" |
| "a number of" | "several" or the actual count |
| "in the case of" | "for" or "when" |
| "is able to" | "can" |
| "has the ability to" | "can" |
| "prior to" | "before" |
| "subsequent to" | "after" |
| "with respect to" | "for" or "about" |
| "in terms of" | rephrase directly |
| "the fact that" | delete or use "that" |

## Sentence structure antipatterns

### Weak openings
Avoid starting sentences with "It is", "There is/are", "This is". Use a concrete subject.

**Bad:** `There are three hooks that the engine attaches to.`
**Good:** `The engine attaches to three hooks.`

### Evidence without a subject
Evidence sentences need an actor or object before the measurement. A sentence that starts from a run ID, script, output path, or table-production step reads like a lab notebook rather than a paper.

**Bad:** `R320 reports higher precision@5 than the flat baseline.`
**Bad:** `The generated table shows that operation stacks reduce inspection work.`
**Good:** `Operation stacks reduce inspection work while preserving localization precision, as the main ranking experiment shows.`

For progress summaries, use the same rule. Say what the paper now claims and what evidence supports it before mentioning how the evidence was produced.

### Project-report prose
Do not let the paper inherit the workflow shape of the project. Run IDs, generated paths, check names, and artifact filenames are useful for reproducibility, but they are not the paper's argument.

**Bad:** `R400 adds a field-suitability report with five rules and passes all checks.`
**Good:** `Field derivation is useful only as a guarded profile-configuration step because deterministic mappings help compression, rank features require ablation guards, and boundary-derived fields need family-specific suitability checks.`

### Too many small experiments
Top-conference evaluation sections need a few substantial experiments tied to claims. If the prose enumerates many tiny checks, consolidate them into 3-4 research questions and use the small checks as supporting evidence.

**Bad:** `We run R320 for ranking, R325 for depth, R358 for boundaries, R366 for fields, and R400 for suitability.`
**Good:** `The evaluation asks whether operation stacks improve localization fidelity and reduce inspection work relative to flat and fixed trees. It then explains which stack fields drive those gains and bounds the cost of reproducing the analysis.`

### Subject-verb separation (Gopen & Swan)
Keep the grammatical subject within 7 words of its verb. Long intervening clauses force the reader to hold the subject in memory.

**Bad:** `The protocol, which was developed over three years by a distributed team working across four time zones, handles failover.`
**Good:** `The protocol handles failover. A distributed team developed it over three years across four time zones.`

### Topic position / stress position (Gopen & Swan)
Put old/known information at the sentence start (backward link). Put the new, emphatic information at the sentence end (stress position).

**Bad:** `A 40\% reduction in latency results from label caching.`
**Good:** `Label caching reduces latency by 40\%.`

### Dangling modifiers
The modifier must attach to the grammatical subject.

**Bad:** `Using eBPF, the policy is enforced at the kernel level.`
**Good:** `Using eBPF, the engine enforces the policy at the kernel level.`

### Passive voice (when the agent matters)
Passive is fine for methodology when the actor is obvious and irrelevant ("traces were collected"), but use active voice when the actor matters for understanding.

**Bad:** `Labels are propagated by the engine at each system event.`
**Good:** `The engine propagates labels at each system event.`

Exception: verification and judgment steps ("samples were verified", "results were reviewed") must name the actor and criterion even in methodology — an agentless verification claim is unfalsifiable .

### Nominalizations (turning verbs into nouns)
Use the verb form when possible. "make assumption" -> "assume"; "perform analysis" -> "analyze"; "is a requirement" -> "requires".

**Bad:** `The propagation of labels occurs at fork events.`
**Good:** `Labels propagate at fork events.`

### Redundant hedging
One hedge per claim is enough. Remove stacked hedges. Do not hedge your own measurements or established facts.

**Bad:** `This may potentially suggest that the overhead could possibly be acceptable.`
**Good:** `This suggests the overhead is acceptable.`

**Protected hedges — never remove:** a hedge that carries claim scope (`suggest ... on the 12 selected workloads`, `in our setting`, `up to`) is protecting the claim from outrunning its evidence. Removing it creates a logic error worse than the wordiness . Remove the stack, keep one scope-bearing hedge.

### Self-attacking sentences (delete)

The mirror rule of protected hedges. A hedge bounds a claim's scope; a self-attack volunteers a weakness, apology, or defensive aside that no reviewer asked for. Delete self-attacks or move the substance to Limitations.

**Bad (delete):** `though neither is central to the typed-boundary claim`
**Bad (delete):** `We describe the type system informally because a full semantics or soundness proof is beyond scope.`
**Good (keep — scope-bearing hedge):** `on the 12 selected workloads`

**Test to tell them apart**: does the phrase restrict WHAT the claim covers (hedge — keep), or does it concede that the work is weak, incomplete, or apologize for a choice (self-attack — delete, or state the boundary neutrally in Limitations)? Grep candidates: `not central`, `beyond (the )?scope`, `we do not claim`, `only a`, `merely`, `unfortunately`, `admittedly`, defensive `though/although` tails after a claim.

### Vague referents

# LaTeX Bilingual Format

Convert a LaTeX paper so that every English sentence is on its own line, followed by a `% 中文翻译。` comment on the next line.

## Format

```latex
English sentence here.
% 中文翻译在这里。
Next English sentence.
% 下一句中文翻译。
```

## Rules

1. **One English sentence per line.** Split paragraphs into individual sentences.
2. **Chinese translation comment immediately after.** Every English sentence gets a `%` comment with its Chinese translation on the next line.
3. **Do NOT change any English text.** Only reformat line breaks and add `%` comments.
4. **Preserve all LaTeX commands.** Labels, refs, citations, macros, environments — all stay intact.
5. **Skip these environments** — leave them as-is, do not add Chinese:
   - `\begin{table}` ... `\end{table}` (including tabular content)
   - `\begin{figure}` ... `\end{figure}`
   - `\begin{lstlisting}` ... `\end{lstlisting}`
   - `\begin{CCSXML}` ... `\end{CCSXML}`
   - `\begin{itemize}` items — add Chinese after each `\item` line
6. **Section/subsection headers** — add Chinese comment after the header line.
7. **Existing Chinese comments** — replace with new per-sentence translations if the format doesn't match (e.g., old paragraph-level comments).
8. **Figure/table captions** — add Chinese comment after the caption line.

## Process

Work section by section, top to bottom:
1. Abstract
2. Introduction
3. Background and Motivation
4. Design
5. Implementation
6. Evaluation
7. Related Work
8. Conclusion

After each section, compile (`make` or `latexmk`) to verify the output is unchanged (same page count, no errors). The Chinese comments should not affect compilation.

## Translation Quality

- Use natural Chinese, not word-by-word translation
- Technical terms: keep the English term on first use, e.g., "沙箱 (sandbox)"
- System names: keep English (Sandlock, Docker, Landlock)
- Acronyms: keep English (MCP, API, SSH)
- Be concise — the Chinese should be shorter than or equal to the English

2	
3	\setcopyright{none}
4	\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
5	\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
